title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: When they rose from the table, Levin would have liked to follow Kitty into the drawing room, but he was afraid she might dislike it as too obvious a show of attention. He stayed in the little knot of men, taking part in the general conversation, and without looking at Kitty he was aware of her movements, her looks, and where she was in the room.

He kept, at once and without the slightest effort, the promise he had made her — always to think well of all men and to like everyone always. The talk turned to the village commune, which Pestsov regarded as a sort of special principle, calling it the "choral" principle. Levin did not agree with Pestsov, nor with his brother, who had his own attitude — at once admitting and not admitting the significance of the Russian commune. But he talked with them, only trying to reconcile and soften their differences. He had no interest in what he was saying himself, and even less in what they were saying; all he wanted was for them, and for everyone, to be happy and content. He now knew the one thing of importance; and that one thing was first there, in the drawing room, and then began moving across the rooms until it came to a stop at the door. Without turning round he could feel the eyes fixed on him, and the smile, and he could not help turning. She was standing in the doorway with Shtcherbatsky, looking at him.
"I thought you were heading for the piano," he said, going over to her. "That's something I miss in the country — music."
"No; we only came to fetch you and thank you," she said, rewarding him with a smile that was like a gift, "for coming. What do they want to argue about? No one ever convinces anyone, you know."
"Yes, that's true," Levin said; "it generally happens that one argues warmly simply because one can't make out what one's opponent is trying to prove."

Levin had often noticed in discussions between the most intelligent people that after enormous effort, and an enormous expenditure of logical subtleties and words, the disputants finally realized that what they had been struggling so long to prove to each other had been known to both of them from the beginning, but that they liked different things and would not say what they liked for fear it would be attacked. He had often experienced suddenly, in the middle of an argument, grasping what it was his opponent liked and at once liking it himself, and immediately finding himself in agreement, after which all the arguments fell away as useless. Sometimes he had had the opposite experience: he had finally come out with what he himself liked, which he had been devising arguments to defend, and, by chance hitting on a happy and sincere phrase for it, had found his opponent agreeing on the spot and dropping the dispute. He tried to say this.
She furrowed her brow, trying to follow him. But the moment he began to illustrate the point with an example, she understood at once.
"I see: one has to find out what he is arguing for, what is precious to him, then one can...."

She had grasped completely and put into words his clumsily expressed idea. Levin smiled joyfully; he was struck by the leap from the muddled, wordy debate with Pestsov and his brother to this brief, clear, almost wordless communication of the most complex ideas.
Shtcherbatsky moved away from them, and Kitty, walking over to a card table, sat down, picked up the chalk, and began drawing diverging circles on the new green cloth.

They went back to the subject that had been raised at dinner — the freedom and occupations of women. Levin agreed with Darya Alexandrovna that a girl who did not marry should find a woman's duties within a family. He supported this by pointing out that no family can manage without women's help; that in every family, poor or rich, there must be nurses, either relatives or hired.
"No," Kitty said, blushing but looking at him all the more boldly with her truthful eyes; "a girl may be so placed that she can't live in the family without humiliation, while she herself...."
He caught her meaning at once.
"Oh, yes," he said. "Yes, yes, yes — you're right; you're right!"

And he saw all that Pestsov had been arguing at dinner about the freedom of women, simply from a glimpse of the terror of an old maid's life and its humiliation in Kitty's heart; and loving her, he felt that terror and humiliation, and at once gave up his arguments.

A silence fell. She was still drawing with the chalk on the table. Her eyes were shining with a soft light. Under the spell of her mood he felt in his whole being a steadily growing tension of happiness.
"Ah! I've scribbled all over the table!" she said, and laying down the chalk, made a movement as if to get up.

"What! Am I to be left alone — without her?" he thought in horror, and he picked up the chalk. "Wait a minute," he said, sitting down at the table. "There's something I've been wanting to ask you for a long time."
He looked straight into her caressing, though frightened, eyes.
"Please, ask it."

"Here," he said; and he wrote the initial letters, _w, y, t, m, i, c, n, b, d, t, m, n, o, t_. These letters meant: "When you told me it could never be, did that mean never, or then?" There seemed no likelihood that she could make out this complicated sentence; but he looked at her as though his life depended on her understanding it. She glanced at him seriously, then leaned her puckered brow on her hands and began to read. Once or twice she stole a glance at him, as if asking, "Is it what I think?"
"I understand," she said, flushing slightly.
"What is this word?" he said, pointing to the _n_ that stood for _never_.
"It means _never_," she said; "but that's not true!"
He quickly rubbed out what he had written, handed her the chalk, and stood up. She wrote, _t, i, c, n, a, d_.

Dolly was entirely comforted from the depression caused by her talk with Alexey Alexandrovitch when she caught sight of the two figures: Kitty with the chalk in her hand, looking up at Levin with a shy and happy smile, and his handsome figure bending over the table, his glowing eyes one moment on the table and the next on her. Suddenly he was radiant: he had understood. It meant, "Then I could not have answered differently."
He glanced at her questioningly, timidly.
"Only then?"
"Yes," her smile answered.
"And n... and now?" he asked.
"Well, read this. I'll tell you what I would like — would like so much!" She wrote the initial letters, _i, y, c, f, a, f, w, h._ This meant, "If you could forget and forgive what happened."
He snatched up the chalk with nervous, trembling fingers, breaking it, and wrote the initial letters of the following: "I have nothing to forget and to forgive; I have never ceased to love you."
She glanced at him with a smile that did not waver.
"I understand," she said in a whisper.
He sat down and wrote a long phrase. She understood it all and, without asking "Is it this?" took the chalk and answered at once.

For a long while he could not make out what she had written, and kept looking into her eyes. He was stupefied with happiness. He could not supply the word she had meant; but in her charming eyes, beaming with happiness, he saw everything he needed to know. And he wrote three letters. But he had barely finished writing when she read them over his arm, and herself finished and wrote the answer: "Yes."
"Playing _secrétaire_?" said the old prince. "But we really must be off if you want to be in time for the theater."
Levin got up and walked Kitty to the door.
In their conversation everything had been said; it had been said that she loved him, and that she would tell her father and mother that he would come tomorrow morning.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: When Kitty had gone and Levin was left alone, he felt such restlessness without her, and such an impatient longing to get as quickly, as quickly as possible, to tomorrow morning, when he would see her again and be bound to her forever, that he was afraid, as of death, of the fourteen hours he had to get through without her. He had to be with someone he could talk to, so as not to be left alone, to kill the time. Stepan Arkadyevitch would have been the most congenial company, but he was going out, he said, to a _soirée_ — really to the ballet. Levin had time only to tell him he was happy, and that he loved him, and would never, never forget what he had done for him. The eyes and the smile of Stepan Arkadyevitch showed Levin that he took in that feeling fittingly.
"Oh, so it's not time to die just yet?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, gripping Levin's hand with feeling.
"N-n-no!" Levin said.

Darya Alexandrovna too, as she said good-bye to him, gave him a sort of congratulation, saying, "How glad I am that you've met Kitty again! One must value old friends." Levin did not like those words of Darya Alexandrovna's. She could not understand how lofty and beyond her this all was, and she ought not to have dared to allude to it. Levin said good-bye to them, but, in order not to be left alone, attached himself to his brother.
"Where are you off to?"
"I'm going to a meeting."
"Well, I'll come along. May I?"
"What for? Yes, come on," said Sergey Ivanovitch, smiling. "What's gotten into you today?"

"Me? Happiness is what's the matter with me!" Levin said, letting down the window of the carriage they were riding in. "You don't mind? — it's so stifling. It's happiness that's the matter with me! Why is it you have never married?"
Sergey Ivanovitch smiled.
"I am very glad — she seems a nice gi...." Sergey Ivanovitch was beginning.

"Don't say it! Don't say it!" Levin shouted, gripping the collar of his fur coat with both hands and muffling him up in it. "'She's a nice girl' — such plain, modest words, so out of harmony with what I feel!"
Sergey Ivanovitch laughed outright with a merry laugh, which was rare with him. "Well, anyway, I may at least say that I'm very glad of it."

"You may do that tomorrow, tomorrow, and nothing more! Nothing, nothing — silence," said Levin, and once more muffling him up in his fur coat, he added: "I do like you so! Well, may I really be present at the meeting?"
"Of course you may."
"What are you discussing today?" Levin asked, never stopping smiling.

They arrived at the meeting. Levin heard the secretary hesitantly read the minutes, which he plainly did not understand himself; but Levin could see from the secretary's face what a good, nice, kind-hearted person he was. That was clear from his confusion and embarrassment as he read the minutes. Then the discussion began. They were arguing about the misappropriation of certain sums and the laying of certain pipes, and Sergey Ivanovitch was very cutting toward two members and said something at length with an air of triumph; another member, scribbling something on a scrap of paper, began timidly at first, but then answered him very viciously and delightfully. And then Sviazhsky (he was there too) said something as well, very handsomely and nobly. Levin listened to them and saw clearly that these missing sums and these pipes were nothing real, and that they were not really angry — they were all the nicest, kindest people, and everything was as cheerful and pleasant as possible among them. They were doing no harm to anyone and were all enjoying themselves. What struck Levin was that today he could see through all of them, and from tiny, almost imperceptible signs could read the soul of each one, and could see clearly that they were all good at heart. And Levin himself in particular they were all extremely fond of that day. That was plain from the way they spoke to him, from the friendly, affectionate looks even those he didn't know gave him.
"Well, did you like it?" Sergey Ivanovitch asked him.
"Very much. I never supposed it would be so interesting! Capital! Splendid!"

Sviazhsky came up to Levin and invited him to come round for tea. Levin could not for the life of him recall or grasp what it was he had disliked in Sviazhsky, what he had failed to find in him. He was a clever and wonderfully good-hearted man.

"Most delighted," he said, and asked after his wife and sister-in-law. And from a queer association of ideas — because in his imagination the idea of Sviazhsky's sister-in-law was linked with marriage — it occurred to him that there was no one to whom he could more fittingly speak of his happiness, and he was very glad to go and see them.

Sviazhsky asked him about the improvements on his estate, taking for granted, as he always did, that there could be no possibility of doing anything that hadn't already been done in Europe — and now this did not annoy Levin in the least. On the contrary, he felt that Sviazhsky was right, that the whole business was of little value, and he could see the wonderful gentleness and tact with which Sviazhsky avoided pressing his correct view fully. The ladies of the Sviazhsky household were particularly delightful. It seemed to Levin that they already knew everything about it and sympathized with him, saying nothing only out of delicacy. He stayed with them an hour, two, three, talking of all sorts of subjects but the one thing that filled his heart, and did not notice that he was boring them dreadfully and that it was long past their bedtime.

Sviazhsky walked him into the hall, yawning and wondering at the strange mood his friend was in. It was past one o'clock. Levin went back to his hotel and was dismayed at the thought that, all alone now with his impatience, he had ten more hours to get through. The servant whose turn it was to be up all night lit his candles and would have gone away, but Levin stopped him. This servant, Yegor, whom Levin had noticed before, struck him as a very intelligent, excellent, and above all good-hearted man.
"Well, Yegor, it's hard going without sleep, isn't it?"
"One has to put up with it! It's part of our work, you see. In a gentleman's house it's easier, but you make more here."
It turned out that Yegor had a family — three boys and a daughter, a seamstress, whom he was hoping to marry to a cashier in a saddler's shop.
Hearing this, Levin informed Yegor that, in his opinion, the great thing in marriage was love, and that with love one would always be happy, because happiness depends only on oneself.

Yegor listened carefully and obviously took in Levin's idea fully, but by way of agreeing with it he produced, much to Levin's surprise, the observation that when he had lived with good masters he had always been satisfied with his masters, and now was perfectly satisfied with his employer, though he was a Frenchman.
"Wonderfully good-hearted fellow!" Levin thought.
"But what about you yourself, Yegor — when you got married, did you love your wife?"
"Ay, why not?" answered Yegor.
And Levin saw that Yegor too was in an excited state and meant to pour out all his deepest feelings.
"My life, too, has been a remarkable one. From the time I was a child...." he was beginning, with flashing eyes, evidently catching Levin's enthusiasm just as people catch yawning.

But at that moment a bell rang. Yegor departed, and Levin was left alone. He had eaten next to nothing at dinner, had refused tea and supper at Sviazhsky's, but he was incapable of thinking about supper. He had not slept the night before, but he could not think about sleep either. His room was cold, but he was overcome by heat. He opened both panes of his window and sat down at the table opposite them. Above the snow-covered roofs you could make out a decorated cross with chains, and above it the rising triangle of Charles's Wain with the yellowish light of Capella. He gazed at the cross, then at the stars, drinking in the fresh freezing air that streamed evenly into the room, and followed, as in a dream, the images and memories that rose in his imagination. At four o'clock he heard footsteps in the passage and peeped out the door. It was Myaskin, the gambler he knew, coming back from the club. He walked gloomily, frowning and coughing. "Poor, unlucky fellow!" Levin thought, and tears came into his eyes from love and pity for this man. He would have spoken with him, and tried to comfort him, but remembering that he had nothing on but his shirt, he changed his mind and sat down again at the open pane to bathe in the cold air and gaze at the exquisite lines of the cross, silent but full of meaning for him, and at the rising lurid yellow star. By seven o'clock there were sounds of floor-polishers at work, and bells ringing somewhere in the servants' quarters, and Levin felt he was beginning to freeze. He shut the pane, washed, dressed, and went out into the street.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The streets were still empty. Levin walked over to the Shtcherbatskys' house. The front doors were closed and everything was asleep. He walked back, returned to his room, and asked for coffee. The day servant, not Yegor this time, brought it to him. Levin would have struck up a conversation with him, but a bell rang for the servant and he went out. Levin tried to drink coffee and put a roll in his mouth, but his mouth simply had no idea what to do with the roll. He rejected the roll, put on his coat, and went out for another walk. It was nine o'clock when he reached the Shtcherbatskys' steps a second time. In the house they were only just up, and the cook came out to go to market. He had at least two more hours to get through.

Through all that night and morning Levin had been living completely unconsciously, feeling lifted out of the conditions of material life altogether. He had eaten nothing for a whole day, had not slept for two nights, had spent several hours half-undressed in the freezing air — and felt not merely fresher and stronger than ever, but altogether independent of his body; he moved without any muscular effort and felt as though he could do anything. He was convinced that he could fly up into the air or lift the corner of the house if need be. He spent the remainder of the time on the street, constantly looking at his watch and gazing about him.

And what he saw then he never saw again afterwards. The children, especially, going to school, the bluish doves flying down from the rooftops to the pavement, and the little loaves dusted with flour, pushed out by an unseen hand — these things touched him. Those loaves, those doves, and those two boys were not creatures of this earth. It all happened at the same instant: a boy ran toward a dove and looked up at Levin, smiling; the dove, with a whir of her wings, darted away, flashing in the sun amid grains of snow that quivered in the air, while from a little window came the smell of fresh-baked bread, and the loaves were put out. All this together was so extraordinarily lovely that Levin laughed and cried with delight. Taking a long roundabout route through Gazetny Place and Kislovka, he went back to the hotel, and setting his watch in front of him, sat down to wait for twelve o'clock. In the next room they were talking about some kind of machines and about swindling, and coughing their morning coughs. They did not realize that the hand was near twelve. The hand reached it. Levin walked out onto the steps. The sledge drivers clearly knew all about it. They crowded round Levin with happy faces, quarreling among themselves and offering their services. Trying not to offend the others, and promising to drive with them too, Levin took one and told him to drive to the Shtcherbatskys'. The sledge driver was splendid, with a white shirt collar sticking out over his overcoat and into his strong, full-blooded red neck. The sledge was high and comfortable, the sort Levin never drove in afterwards, and the horse was a good one, and tried to gallop yet didn't seem to be moving. The driver knew the Shtcherbatskys' house, and drew up at the entrance with a flourish of his arm and a "Wo!" expressly indicating his respect for his fare. The Shtcherbatskys' hall-porter certainly knew all about it. That was plain from the smile in his eyes and the way he said:
"It's been a long time since you came to see us, Konstantin Dmitrievitch!"
Not only did he know all about it — he was unmistakably delighted and trying to hide his joy. Looking into his kindly old eyes, Levin realized something new in his happiness.
"Are they up?"
"Pray walk in! Leave it here," he said, smiling, as Levin would have come back for his hat. That meant something.
"Whom shall I announce to her honor?" asked the footman.
The footman, though a young man and one of the new school of footmen, a dandy, was a very kind-hearted, decent fellow, and he too knew all about it.
"The princess ... the prince ... the young princess...." said Levin.

The first person he saw was Mademoiselle Linon. She walked across the room, and her ringlets and her face were beaming. He had barely spoken to her when he suddenly heard the rustle of a skirt at the door, and Mademoiselle Linon vanished from Levin's sight, and a joyful terror came over him at the nearness of his happiness. Mademoiselle Linon was in a great hurry, and leaving him, went out by the other door. The moment she was gone, swift, swift light steps sounded on the parquet, and his bliss, his life, himself — what was best in himself, what he had so long sought and longed for — was quickly, so quickly approaching him. She did not walk so much as float, by some invisible force, toward him. He saw nothing but her clear, truthful eyes, frightened by the same bliss of love that flooded his own heart. Those eyes shone nearer and nearer, blinding him with their light of love. She stopped close to him, touching him. Her hands rose and dropped onto his shoulders.
She had done all she could — she had run up to him and given herself over entirely, shy and happy. He put his arms around her and pressed his lips to her mouth that sought his kiss.
She, too, had not slept all night, and had been expecting him all morning.

Her mother and father had agreed without demur and were happy in her happiness. She had been waiting for him. She had wanted to be the first to tell him her happiness and his. She had got herself ready to see him alone, and had been delighted at the prospect, and shy and ashamed, and did not know herself what she was doing. She had heard his steps and voice and had waited at the door for Mademoiselle Linon to leave. Mademoiselle Linon had gone. Without thinking, without asking herself how or what, she had gone up to him and done what she did.

"Let's go to mamma!" she said, taking him by the hand. For a long while he could say nothing — not so much because he was afraid of desecrating the loftiness of his emotion with a word, as because every time he tried to speak, instead of words he felt tears of happiness welling up. He took her hand and kissed it.
"Can it really be true?" he said at last in a choked voice. "I cannot believe you love me, my dear!"
She smiled at that "dear," and at the shyness with which he glanced at her.
"Yes!" she said meaningfully, deliberately. "I am so happy!"

Not letting go of his hands, she went into the drawing room. The princess, seeing them, breathed quickly and immediately began to cry, and then immediately began to laugh, and with a vigorous step Levin had not expected from her, ran up to him and, hugging his head, kissed him, wetting his cheeks with her tears.
"So it's all settled! I am glad. Love her. I am glad.... Kitty!"
"You haven't been long settling things," said the old prince, trying to seem unmoved; but Levin noticed that his eyes were wet when he turned to him.
"I have long, always wanted this!" said the prince, taking Levin by the arm and drawing him toward himself. "Even when this little featherhead fancied...."
"Papa!" shrieked Kitty, and shut his mouth with her hands.
"All right, I won't!" he said. "I'm very, very ... plea... Oh, what a fool I am...."
He embraced Kitty, kissed her face, her hand, her face again, and made the sign of the cross over her.
And a new feeling of love came over Levin for this man, until then so little known to him, when he saw how slowly and tenderly Kitty kissed his muscular hand.

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: The princess sat in her armchair, silent and smiling; the prince sat down beside her. Kitty stood by her father's chair, still holding his hand. No one spoke.
It was the princess who first put everything into words, translating thoughts and feelings into practical questions. And to all of them, for the first minute, that felt strange and almost painful.
"When is it to be? We have to arrange the blessing and the announcement. And when will the wedding be? What do you say, Alexander?"
"There he is," said the old prince, gesturing toward Levin. "He's the chief person in this business."
"When?" said Levin, blushing. "Tomorrow. If you ask me, the blessing today and the wedding tomorrow."
"Come now, _mon cher_, don't be absurd!"
"Well — in a week, then."
"He's out of his mind."
"No — why is that?"
"Well, I never!" said the mother, smiling, pleased by his eagerness. "And what about the trousseau?"

"Will there really have to be a trousseau and all the rest of it?" Levin thought, horrified. "But can a trousseau and a blessing and all that — can any of it spoil my happiness? Nothing can spoil it." He glanced at Kitty and saw that she was not in the least, not in the slightest, troubled by the question of the trousseau. "Then it must be all right," he thought.
"I don't know anything about it; I was only saying what I'd like," he said apologetically.
"We'll talk it through, then. The blessing and the announcement can happen now. That's very good."

The princess went over to her husband, kissed him, and was about to leave, but he held her back, embraced her, and — as tenderly as a young lover — kissed her several times, smiling. The two old people were briefly muddled and seemed unsure whether it was they who were in love again or their daughter. Once they had gone, Levin went up to his fiancée and took her hand. He was composed now and could speak, and there was a great deal he wanted to tell her. But what came out wasn't what he had meant to say at all.
"How I knew it would turn out this way! I never let myself hope for it, and yet inside I was always certain," he said. "I believe it was meant to be."

"And so did I!" she said. "Even when...." She stopped, then went on, looking at him steadily with her honest eyes, "Even when I pushed my own happiness away. I always loved only you, but I got carried away. I have to tell you.... Can you forgive that?"
"Maybe it was for the best. You'll have so much of mine to forgive. I have to tell you...."

This was one of the things he had been meaning to bring up. He had decided from the start to tell her two things — that he wasn't pure as she was, and that he wasn't a believer. It was agonizing, but he felt he owed her both admissions.
"No, not now — later!" he said.
"All right, later, but you must tell me. I'm not afraid of anything. I want to know everything. Now it's settled."
He added: "Settled that you'll take me whatever I turn out to be — that you won't give me up? Yes?"
"Yes, yes."

Their conversation was broken off by Mademoiselle Linon, who came in with a put-on but tender smile to congratulate her favorite pupil. Before she had gone, the servants arrived with their congratulations. Then relatives turned up, and there began the state of blissful confusion that Levin did not emerge from until the day after the wedding. He felt constantly awkward and uncomfortable, but the intensity of his happiness kept on growing. He sensed that a great deal was being expected of him — what exactly, he couldn't say; he did everything he was told, and all of it made him happy. He had imagined his engagement would be unlike anyone else's, that the ordinary trappings would cheapen his unique happiness; but in the end he did exactly what everyone else did, and his happiness only grew from it, becoming more and more particular, more and more unlike anything that had ever happened before.
"Now we'll need sweets," Mademoiselle Linon announced — and off Levin drove to buy sweets.
"Well, I'm delighted," said Sviazhsky. "I'd recommend getting the bouquets from Fomin's."
"Oh — are bouquets needed?" And he drove off to Fomin's.
His brother offered to lend him money, since there'd be so many expenses, presents to be given....
"Oh — are presents needed?" And he hurried off to Foulde's.

And at the confectioner's, and at Fomin's, and at Foulde's, he saw that he was expected; that they were pleased to see him and took pride in his happiness, just like everyone else he encountered in those days. What was extraordinary was that not only did everyone like him, but even people who had previously been unsympathetic, cold, indifferent, were now enthusiastic about him, gave way to him in everything, handled his feelings with tenderness and tact, and shared his conviction that he was the happiest man in the world because his fiancée was beyond perfection. Kitty felt the same. When Countess Nordston hinted that she had hoped for something better, Kitty grew so indignant and argued so convincingly that nothing in the world could be better than Levin, that Countess Nordston was forced to concede the point, and never met him in Kitty's company again without a smile of rapturous admiration.

The confession he had promised her was the one painful episode of this time. He consulted the old prince, and with his approval gave Kitty the diary in which he had written down the confession that tormented him. He had kept this diary at the time precisely with a future wife in mind. Two things gave him anguish: his lack of purity and his lack of faith. The confession of unbelief passed without remark. She was religious, had never questioned the truths of religion, but his outward unbelief didn't trouble her at all. Through love she knew his whole soul, and in his soul she saw what she wanted, and the fact that such a soul might be called unbelieving meant nothing to her. The other confession set her weeping bitterly.

It was not without inner struggle that Levin handed her the diary. He knew that there couldn't and shouldn't be secrets between them, and so he had decided that this was how it had to be. But he hadn't grasped the effect it would have on her — he hadn't put himself in her place. It was only that same evening, when he came over before the theater, went into her room and saw her tear-streaked, pitiful, sweet face, miserable with a pain he had caused and could never undo, that he felt the abyss between his shameful past and her dovelike purity, and was horrified at what he had done.

"Take them — take these dreadful books away!" she said, pushing the notebooks aside on the table. "Why did you give them to me? No — it was better this way, all the same," she added, moved by his despairing face. "But it's awful, awful!"
He bowed his head and said nothing. There was nothing he could say.
"You can't forgive me," he whispered.
"Yes — I forgive you; but it's terrible!"

But his happiness was so immense that this confession didn't shatter it; it only added another shade to it. She forgave him; but from then on he considered himself even less worthy of her, bowed lower in spirit than ever before her, and prized his undeserved happiness more highly than ever.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Without meaning to, Alexey Alexandrovitch went back over the conversations during and after dinner as he returned to his solitary room. Darya Alexandrovna's words about forgiveness had only irritated him. Whether the Christian precept applied to his case was too difficult a question to be tossed around in passing, and besides, he had long ago settled it for himself in the negative. Of everything that had been said, what stuck in his memory was the line from that stupid, good-natured Turovtsin — "_Acted like a man, he did! Called him out and shot him!_" Everyone, apparently, had felt the same, even if politeness kept them from saying so.

"But the matter is settled, there's no point dwelling on it," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself. Thinking only of the journey ahead and the revision work he had to do, he went into his room and asked the porter who had shown him up where his valet was. The porter answered that the man had only just stepped out. Alexey Alexandrovitch ordered tea brought to him, sat down at the table, took the guidebook, and began going over the route of his journey.
"Two telegrams," said his valet, coming into the room. "I beg your pardon, your excellency — I'd only just stepped out for a minute."

Alexey Alexandrovitch took the telegrams and opened them. The first announced Stremov's appointment to the very post that Karenin had wanted. He threw the telegram down and, flushing slightly, got up and began to pace the room. "_Quos vult perdere dementat_," he said, meaning by _quos_ those responsible for the appointment. It wasn't so much that he hadn't been given the post, or that he had been pointedly passed over; what astonished him was that they couldn't see how the wordy phrase-monger Stremov was the last man fit for it. How could they fail to notice that they were undermining themselves and damaging their own _prestige_ with this choice?

"More of the same," he muttered bitterly, opening the second telegram. The telegram was from his wife. Her name, written in blue pencil — "Anna" — was the first thing his eye caught. "I am dying; I beg, I implore you to come. I shall die easier with your forgiveness," he read. He smiled contemptuously and threw the telegram down. That this was a trick and a fraud, of that, he thought for the first moment, there could be no doubt.

"There's no deceit she wouldn't stoop to. She was near her confinement. Perhaps it is the confinement. But what would they be after? To legitimize the child, to compromise me, and block the divorce," he thought. "But there was something in it: I am dying...." He read the telegram again, and suddenly the plain meaning of the words struck him.

"And what if it's true?" he said to himself. "If it's true that at the moment of agony, of nearness to death, she really is repentant, and I treat it as a trick and refuse to go? That wouldn't only be cruel — and everyone would blame me — it would be foolish of me."
"Piotr, call a coach — I'm going to Petersburg," he said to his servant.

Alexey Alexandrovitch resolved that he would go to Petersburg and see his wife. If her illness turned out to be a trick, he would say nothing and leave again. If she really was in danger and wanted to see him before she died, he would forgive her if he found her alive and pay her the last respects if he was too late.
On the whole journey he gave no further thought to what he ought to do.

Weary and unclean from a night spent in the train, in the early morning fog of Petersburg, Alexey Alexandrovitch drove along the deserted Nevsky, staring straight ahead, not thinking about what awaited him. He could not bring himself to think about it, because every time he pictured what would happen, he couldn't push away the recognition that her death would at once remove every difficulty in his position. Bakers, shuttered shops, night cabbies, porters sweeping the pavements all flashed past, and he watched it all, trying to smother the thought of what was ahead and what he didn't dare hope for — and yet was hoping for. He drove up to the steps. A sledge and a carriage with a sleeping coachman stood at the entrance. As he stepped into the hall, Alexey Alexandrovitch fished out, as it were, from the farthest corner of his brain his resolve, and made himself fully master of it. Its substance ran: "If it's a trick, then calm contempt, and leave. If it's true, do what's proper."
The porter opened the door before Alexey Alexandrovitch could ring. The porter, Kapitonitch, looked odd in an old coat, without a tie, and in slippers.
"How is your mistress?"
"A successful confinement yesterday."
Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped short and went white. He felt, distinctly now, how intensely he had been hoping for her death.
"And how is she?"
Korney, in his morning apron, came hurrying down the stairs.
"Very ill," he answered. "There was a consultation yesterday, and the doctor is here now."
"Take my things," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, and, feeling a slight relief at the news that there was still some hope of her death, he stepped into the hall.
On the hat-stand was a military overcoat. Alexey Alexandrovitch noticed it and asked:
"Who is here?"
"The doctor, the midwife, and Count Vronsky."
Alexey Alexandrovitch walked through into the inner rooms.
There was no one in the drawing-room; at the sound of his footsteps, the midwife came out of Anna's boudoir, in a cap with lilac ribbons.
She went up to Alexey Alexandrovitch and, with the familiarity that the nearness of death allows, took him by the arm and drew him toward the bedroom.
"Thank God you've come! She talks of nothing but you," she said.
"Bring the ice — quickly!" came the doctor's curt voice from the bedroom.
Alexey Alexandrovitch went into her boudoir.

At the table, sitting sideways in a low chair, was Vronsky, his face buried in his hands, weeping. At the sound of the doctor's voice he jumped up, lowered his hands, and saw Alexey Alexandrovitch. At the sight of the husband, he was so stricken that he sat down again, pulling his head down between his shoulders as if he wanted to vanish; but he forced himself, stood up, and said:
"She is dying. The doctors say there is no hope. I am entirely in your power, only let me stay here.... I'm at your disposal. I...."

Alexey Alexandrovitch, seeing Vronsky's tears, felt that rush of nervous emotion that the suffering of others always stirred in him; turning his face away, he hurried toward the door without waiting to hear the rest. From the bedroom came the sound of Anna's voice saying something. Her voice was lively, eager, with strikingly clear intonations. Alexey Alexandrovitch entered the bedroom and went up to the bed. She was lying with her face turned toward him. Her cheeks were flushed crimson, her eyes glittered, her little white hands, thrust out from the sleeves of her dressing-gown, played with the quilt, twisting it in her fingers. She looked not only well and blooming but in the happiest frame of mind. She was talking quickly, musically, with unusually precise articulation and expressive intonation.

"For Alexey — I mean Alexey Alexandrovitch (what a strange and dreadful thing it is, that both of them are Alexey, isn't it?) — Alexey wouldn't refuse me. I should forget; he would forgive.... But why doesn't he come? He's so good he doesn't even know how good he is. Oh, my God, what agony! Quick — give me some water! Oh, that will be bad for her, my little girl! All right then, give her to a nurse. Yes, I agree, that really is better. He'll be coming; it will hurt him to see her. Give her to the nurse."
"Anna Arkadyevna, he has come. Here he is!" said the midwife, trying to draw her attention to Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"Oh, what nonsense!" Anna went on, not seeing her husband. "No, give her to me — give me my little one! He hasn't come yet. You say he won't forgive me, because you don't know him. Nobody knows him. Only I do, and even for me it was hard. His eyes — I should know them — Seryozha has just the same eyes — and I can't bear to look at them because of it. Has Seryozha had his dinner? I know everyone will forget about him. He would not forget. Seryozha must be moved into the corner room, and Mariette must be asked to sleep with him."
Suddenly she shrank back, fell silent; and in terror, as if expecting a blow, as if shielding herself, she raised her hands to her face. She had seen her husband.

"No, no!" she said. "I'm not afraid of him; I'm afraid of death. Alexey, come here. I'm in a hurry, because I have no time, I have not long to live; the fever will start any minute and I'll understand nothing more. Right now I understand, I understand everything, I see it all!"

Alexey Alexandrovitch's lined face wore an expression of agony; he took her by the hand and tried to say something, but couldn't get the words out; his lower lip trembled, but he kept on wrestling with his emotion and only glanced at her now and then. And each time he glanced at her, he saw her eyes resting on him with a passionate, triumphant tenderness he had never seen in them before.

"Wait a minute, you don't know.... Stay a little, stay!..." She paused, as if gathering her thoughts. "Yes," she began; "yes, yes, yes. This is what I wanted to say. Don't be surprised at me. I'm still the same.... But there is another woman in me, I'm afraid of her: she loved that man, and I tried to hate you, and couldn't forget about the woman I used to be. I'm not her. Now I'm my real self, all of me. I'm dying now — I know I'm going to die, ask him. Even now I can feel — see, the weights on my feet, on my hands, on my fingers. My fingers — see how huge they are! But this will all be over soon.... Only one thing I want: forgive me, forgive me completely. I'm terrible, but my old nurse used to tell me about that holy martyr — what was her name? She was worse. And I'll go to Rome; there's a wilderness there, and I'll be no trouble to anyone, only I'll take Seryozha and the little one.... No, you can't forgive me! I know — it can't be forgiven! No, no, go away, you're too good!" She held his hand in one burning hand, while she pushed him away with the other.

Alexey Alexandrovitch's nervous agitation kept rising, until he stopped struggling against it. He suddenly felt that what he had thought of as nervous agitation was on the contrary a blissful spiritual state that gave him, all at once, a new happiness he had never known. He didn't think that the Christian law he had been trying to live by all his life commanded him to forgive and love his enemies; but a glad feeling of love and forgiveness toward his enemies filled his heart. He knelt down and, laying his head in the bend of her arm, which burned him through the sleeve as though with fire, he sobbed like a small child. She put her arm around his head, drew him closer, and with defiant pride raised her eyes.
"There he is. I knew him! Now, forgive me, everyone, forgive me!... They've come again — why don't they leave?... Oh, take these cloaks off me!"
The doctor loosened her hands, settled her carefully on the pillow, and covered her up to the shoulders. She lay back submissively and looked ahead of her with shining eyes.

"Remember one thing — that all I needed was forgiveness, and I want nothing more.... Why doesn't _he_ come?" she said, turning toward the door where Vronsky stood. "Do come, do come! Give him your hand."
Vronsky came up to the side of the bed and, seeing Anna, hid his face in his hands again.
"Uncover your face — look at him! He's a saint," she said. "Oh — uncover your face, do!" she said angrily. "Alexey Alexandrovitch, do uncover his face! I want to see him."
Alexey Alexandrovitch took Vronsky's hands and drew them away from his face, which was dreadful with the expression of agony and shame on it.
"Give him your hand. Forgive him."
Alexey Alexandrovitch held out his hand, not trying to hold back the tears that streamed from his eyes.

"Thank God, thank God!" she said, "now everything is ready. Just to stretch my legs a little. There — that's lovely. How badly these flowers are done — they don't look like violets at all," she said, pointing to the hangings. "My God, my God! When will it end? Give me some morphine. Doctor, give me some morphine! Oh, my God, my God!"
And she tossed about on the bed.

The doctors said it was puerperal fever, and that there were ninety-nine chances out of a hundred that it would end in death. All day long there was fever, delirium, and loss of consciousness. By midnight the patient lay unconscious, and almost without pulse.
The end was expected at any moment.

Vronsky had gone home, but in the morning he came back to inquire, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, meeting him in the hall, said: "You'd better stay; she might ask for you," and led him himself to his wife's boudoir. Toward morning there was a return of the excitement, the rapid thought and talk, and again it ended in unconsciousness. On the third day it was the same, and the doctors said there was hope. That day Alexey Alexandrovitch went into the boudoir where Vronsky was sitting, shut the door, and sat down opposite him.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch," said Vronsky, sensing that some statement of the situation was coming, "I can't speak, I can't take it in. Spare me! However hard it is for you, believe me, it is more terrible for me."
He would have stood up, but Alexey Alexandrovitch took him by the hand and said:

"Please hear me out — it's necessary. I have to explain my feelings, the feelings that have guided me and will guide me, so that you won't be in any doubt about me. You know that I had resolved on a divorce and had even begun proceedings. I won't hide from you that when I started this, I was full of uncertainty, full of misery; I'll admit that I was pursued by a desire to take revenge on you and on her. When I got the telegram, I came here with the same feelings; I'll say more — I longed for her death. But...." He paused, weighing whether to reveal what he felt to him. "But I saw her and forgave her. And the happiness of forgiveness has revealed my duty to me. I forgive completely. I would offer the other cheek, I would give my cloak if my coat were taken. I only pray to God that he won't take from me the bliss of forgiveness!"
Tears stood in his eyes, and Vronsky was struck by the luminous, serene look in them.

"This is where I stand: you can trample me in the mud, make me the laughing-stock of the world, I will not abandon her, and I will never speak a word of reproach to you," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on. "My duty is clearly laid out for me; I ought to be with her, and I will be. If she wants to see you, I'll let you know, but for now I think it would be better for you to go away."

He stood up, and sobs cut off his words. Vronsky was getting up too, and in a hunched, not yet fully straightened posture, he looked up at him from under his brows. He didn't understand Alexey Alexandrovitch's feeling, but he sensed that it was something higher, and unattainable for him with his view of life.

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: After the conversation with Alexey Alexandrovitch, Vronsky stepped out onto the porch of the Karenins' house and stood there, struggling to remember where he was and where he was supposed to walk or drive. He felt disgraced, humiliated, guilty, and stripped of any possibility of washing the humiliation away. He felt knocked off the well-worn track along which he had so proudly and lightly walked until now. All the habits and rules of his life that had seemed so solid had turned out, all at once, to be false and useless. The betrayed husband, who up to that point had figured as a pitiful creature, an incidental and slightly ridiculous obstacle to his happiness, had suddenly been summoned by Anna herself and lifted to an awe-inspiring height — and from that height the husband had revealed himself, not as malicious, not as false, not as ridiculous, but as kind and straightforward and large. Vronsky couldn't help feeling this, and the roles had abruptly been reversed. He felt the other man's elevation and his own abasement, the other man's truth and his own falsehood. He felt that the husband was magnanimous even in his sorrow, while he had been base and petty in his deceit. But this sense of his own humiliation in front of the man he had unjustly looked down on was only a small part of his misery. He felt unutterably wretched now, because his passion for Anna, which had seemed to him lately to be cooling, was — now that he knew he had lost her forever — stronger than it had ever been. He had seen the whole of her in her illness, had come to know her very soul, and it seemed to him that he had never loved her till then. And now, when he had learned to know her, to love her the way she should be loved, he had been humiliated before her and had lost her forever, leaving her with nothing of himself but a shameful memory. Worst of all was his ridiculous, shameful position when Alexey Alexandrovitch had pulled his hands away from his humiliated face. He stood on the steps of the Karenins' house as though out of his mind, with no idea what to do.
"A sledge, sir?" asked the porter.
"Yes — a sledge."

Once home, after three sleepless nights, Vronsky lay down on the sofa without undressing, clasping his hands and resting his head on them. His head was heavy. Images, memories, ideas of the strangest sort followed each other in his mind with extraordinary speed and clarity. First it was the medicine he had poured out for the patient and spilled over the spoon, then the midwife's white hands, then the strange posture of Alexey Alexandrovitch on the floor beside the bed.

"Sleep! Forget!" he told himself with the calm confidence of a healthy man that if he's tired and sleepy, he'll fall asleep at once. And just then his head did begin to grow drowsy and he began to slip into oblivion. The waves of the sea of unconsciousness had begun to close over his head when — all at once — it felt as though a violent electric shock had passed through him. He started so violently that he leapt up on the springs of the sofa, and bracing himself on his arms, found himself in a panic on his knees. His eyes were wide open, as if he had never been asleep at all. The heaviness in his head and the weariness in his limbs that he had felt a minute before were suddenly gone.

"You can trample me in the mud," he heard Alexey Alexandrovitch saying, and saw him standing in front of him, and saw Anna's face with its burning flush and glittering eyes, gazing with love and tenderness not at him but at Alexey Alexandrovitch; he saw his own — as he imagined it — foolish, ridiculous figure when Alexey Alexandrovitch took his hands away from his face. He stretched out his legs again and threw himself onto the sofa in the same position and shut his eyes.
"Sleep! Forget!" he repeated to himself. But with his eyes closed he saw, more vividly than before, Anna's face as it had been on the memorable evening before the races.

"That isn't and won't be, and she wants to wipe it out of her memory. But I can't live without it. How can we be reconciled? How can we be reconciled?" he said aloud, and without realizing it began repeating the words. The repetition held back the rising tide of fresh images and memories that he could feel crowding into his brain. But the repeating of words didn't hold his imagination back for long. Again, in extraordinarily rapid succession, his best moments rose up before his mind, then his recent humiliation. "Take his hands away," Anna's voice says. He takes them away and feels the shame-struck, idiotic expression of his face.

He went on lying there, trying to sleep, though he knew there wasn't the slightest hope of it, and kept repeating stray words from some chain of thought, trying that way to hold off the rising flood of new images. He listened, and heard, in a strange, mad whisper, the words repeated: "I didn't value it, didn't make enough of it. I didn't value it, didn't make enough of it."

"What is this? Am I losing my mind?" he said to himself. "Maybe. What is it that makes people lose their minds; what makes them shoot themselves?" he answered himself, and opening his eyes, he saw, to his surprise, an embroidered cushion beside him, made by Varya, his brother's wife. He fingered the tassel of the cushion and tried to think of Varya, of when he had last seen her. But thinking of anything outside himself was an agonizing effort. "No, I have to sleep!" He pulled the cushion up and pressed his head into it, but it took an effort to keep his eyes shut. He jumped up and sat down. "That's all finished for me," he told himself. "I have to think what to do. What is left?" His mind ran rapidly over the parts of his life apart from his love for Anna.

"Ambition? Serpuhovskoy? Society? The court?" He couldn't get any of them to hold his attention. All of it had meant something before, but now there was no reality in any of it. He got up from the sofa, took off his coat, undid his belt, and, uncovering his hairy chest to breathe more easily, paced up and down the room. "This is how people go mad," he repeated, "and how they shoot themselves... to escape humiliation," he added slowly.

He went to the door and shut it, then with fixed eyes and clenched teeth he walked over to the table, picked up a revolver, looked around him, turned it to a loaded barrel, and sank into thought. For two minutes, his head bent forward in an expression of intense concentration, he stood with the revolver in his hand, motionless, thinking.

"Of course," he said to himself, as if a logical, continuous, clear chain of reasoning had brought him to an indisputable conclusion. In fact this "of course," which seemed so convincing to him, was simply the result of going around again through exactly the same circle of memories and images that he had already passed through ten times in the last hour — memories of happiness lost forever. There was the same conception of the meaninglessness of everything still to come in life, the same awareness of humiliation. Even the sequence of these images and emotions was the same.

"Of course," he repeated, when for the third time his thought passed around the same spellbound circle of memories and images, and pulling the revolver to the left side of his chest, gripping it firmly with his whole hand, as if squeezing it in his fist, he pulled the trigger. He didn't hear the sound of the shot, but a violent blow to his chest sent him reeling. He tried to clutch the edge of the table, dropped the revolver, staggered, and sat down on the floor, looking around him in astonishment. He didn't recognize his own room as he looked up from the floor at the bent legs of the table, the wastepaper basket, the tiger-skin rug. The hurried, creaking steps of his servant coming through the drawing-room brought him back to himself. He made an effort to think and realized that he was on the floor; and seeing blood on the tiger-skin rug and on his arm, he understood that he had shot himself.

"Idiotic! Missed!" he said, groping for the revolver. The revolver was right beside him — he was reaching farther off. Still feeling for it, he stretched out to the other side, and not having the strength to keep his balance, fell over, streaming with blood.

The elegant, whiskered manservant, who used to complain endlessly to his acquaintances about the delicacy of his nerves, was so panic-stricken at the sight of his master lying on the floor that he left him bleeding while he ran for help. An hour later Varya, his brother's wife, had arrived, and with the help of three doctors she had sent for in all directions, all of whom turned up at the same moment, she got the wounded man into bed and stayed to nurse him.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: The mistake Alexey Alexandrovitch had made — in that, when he had been preparing to see his wife, he had overlooked the possibility that her repentance might be genuine, that he might forgive her, and that she might not die — that mistake came home to him in its full meaning two months after his return from Moscow. But the mistake hadn't arisen only from his having overlooked that possibility; it had also arisen from the fact that, until that day at his dying wife's bedside, he hadn't known his own heart. At her sickbed he had given way, for the first time in his life, to that feeling of sympathetic suffering that the suffering of others always stirred in him, and which he had until then regarded with shame as a harmful weakness. And pity for her, and remorse for having wished her dead, and above all the joy of forgiveness, made him suddenly aware not just of the easing of his own pain, but of a spiritual peace he had never known before. He suddenly felt that the very thing that had been the source of his suffering had become the source of his spiritual joy; that what had seemed insoluble when he was judging, blaming, and hating had become clear and simple once he forgave and loved.

He forgave his wife and pitied her for her suffering and her remorse. He forgave Vronsky and pitied him, especially after the reports of his desperate act reached him. He felt more for his son than before. And he blamed himself now for having taken too little interest in him. But for the little newborn baby he felt a quite particular sentiment — not just pity, but tenderness. At first, out of pure compassion, he had taken an interest in the delicate little creature, who wasn't his child and had been pushed aside during her mother's illness and would certainly have died if he hadn't bothered about her, and he didn't notice himself how attached he was becoming to her. He would go into the nursery several times a day and sit there for a long time, so that the nurses, at first wary of him, got quite used to having him there. Sometimes for half an hour at a stretch he would sit in silence, gazing at the saffron-red, downy, wrinkled face of the sleeping baby, watching the movements of her frowning brows and her fat little hands with their clenched fingers as they rubbed her eyes and nose. At moments like these especially, Alexey Alexandrovitch felt a perfect peace and inner harmony, and saw nothing extraordinary in his position, nothing that needed to change.

But as time went on, he saw more and more clearly that however natural his position now seemed to him, he wouldn't be allowed to stay in it for long. He felt that beyond the blessed spiritual force directing his soul there was another, a brutal force, just as powerful or more so, that controlled his life, and that this force would not permit him the humble peace he longed for. He felt that everyone looked at him with curious astonishment, that he wasn't understood, and that something was expected of him. Above all, he felt the instability and unnaturalness of his relations with his wife.

Once the softening effect of death's near approach had faded, Alexey Alexandrovitch began to notice that Anna was afraid of him, ill at ease in his company, and couldn't meet his eye. She seemed to want, and not dare, to tell him something; and as though sensing that things couldn't go on as they were, she seemed to be waiting for something from him.

Toward the end of February it happened that Anna's baby daughter, who had also been named Anna, fell ill. Alexey Alexandrovitch was in the nursery that morning, and after leaving orders for the doctor to be sent for, he went off to his office. When he had finished his work, he came home at four. Going into the hall, he saw a handsome groom in a braided livery and a bearskin cape, holding a white fur cloak.
"Who is here?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"Princess Elizaveta Federovna Tverskaya," the groom answered, and it seemed to Alexey Alexandrovitch that the man grinned.

All through this difficult time, Alexey Alexandrovitch had noticed that his social acquaintances, especially the women, took a particular interest in him and his wife. All of them, he observed, were poorly hiding their amusement at something — the same amusement he had glimpsed in the lawyer's eyes, and just now in this groom's. Everyone seemed somehow hugely delighted, as if they had just been to a wedding. When they met him, they would ask after his wife's health with ill-concealed enjoyment. The presence of Princess Tverskaya was unpleasant to Alexey Alexandrovitch — because of the memories he associated with her, and because he disliked her — and he went straight to the nursery. In the day nursery, Seryozha, leaning on the table with his legs up on a chair, was drawing and chattering away cheerfully. The English governess, who had taken the place of the French one during Anna's illness, was sitting near the boy, knitting a shawl. She hurriedly stood up, curtsied, and gave Seryozha a tug.
Alexey Alexandrovitch stroked his son's hair, answered the governess's questions about his wife, and asked what the doctor had said about the baby.
"The doctor said it wasn't anything serious, and he prescribed a bath, sir."
"But she's still in pain," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, listening to the baby's screams in the next room.
"I think it's the wet-nurse, sir," the Englishwoman said firmly.
"What makes you say so?" he asked, stopping short.
"It was just like this at Countess Paul's, sir. They gave the baby medicine, and it turned out the baby was simply hungry: the nurse had no milk, sir."

Alexey Alexandrovitch thought it over, and after standing still for a few seconds went in through the other door. The baby was lying with her head thrown back, stiffening herself in the nurse's arms, refusing to take the full breast offered her; and she did not stop screaming despite the double hushing of the wet-nurse and the other nurse, who was leaning over her.
"Still no better?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"She's very restless," the nurse answered in a whisper.
"Miss Edwarde says the wet-nurse may have no milk," he said.
"I think so too, Alexey Alexandrovitch."
"Then why didn't you say so?"
"Who was I to say it to? Anna Arkadyevna still being ill...." said the nurse discontentedly.
The nurse was an old family servant. And in her plain words Alexey Alexandrovitch seemed to hear an allusion to his own situation.
The baby screamed louder than ever, struggling and sobbing. The nurse, with a gesture of despair, went over to her, took her from the wet-nurse's arms, and began walking up and down, rocking her.

"You must ask the doctor to examine the wet-nurse," said Alexey Alexandrovitch. The smartly dressed, healthy-looking nurse, alarmed at the thought of losing her position, muttered something to herself and, covering her bosom, smiled contemptuously at the idea that anyone could doubt the abundance of her milk. In that smile, too, Alexey Alexandrovitch saw a sneer at his situation.
"Poor little thing!" said the nurse, soothing the baby and still pacing with her.
Alexey Alexandrovitch sat down, and with a dejected, suffering face watched the nurse walking back and forth.

When the child was finally quiet and had been laid in her deep cot, and the nurse, after smoothing the little pillow, had left her, Alexey Alexandrovitch got up and, walking awkwardly on tiptoe, approached the baby. He stood still for a minute, gazing at her with the same dejected face; but all at once a smile, moving his hair and the skin of his forehead, broke out over his face, and he stepped just as softly out of the room.

In the dining room he rang the bell and told the servant who answered to send for the doctor again. He felt annoyed with his wife for not being worried about this exquisite baby, and in that annoyed mood he had no wish to go to her; he had no wish, either, to see Princess Betsy. But his wife might wonder why he didn't come in to her as usual, and so, overcoming his reluctance, he started toward the bedroom. As he walked over the soft rug toward the door, he couldn't help overhearing a conversation he didn't want to hear.
"If he hadn't been leaving, I could have understood your answer and his too. But your husband ought to be above that," Betsy was saying.
"It's not because of my husband; for myself I don't want it. Don't say that!" Anna's voice answered, agitated.
"Yes, but you must want to say good-bye to a man who has shot himself on your account...."
"That's exactly why I don't want to."

With a dismayed, guilty look, Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped and would have gone back unseen. But it occurred to him that this would be undignified, and he turned back again, and clearing his throat, walked up to the bedroom. The voices had stopped, and he went in.

Anna, in a gray dressing-gown, with a crop of short clustering black curls on her round head, was sitting on a settee. The eagerness drained from her face, as it always did, at the sight of her husband; she lowered her head and glanced uneasily at Betsy. Betsy, dressed in the height of the latest fashion, in a hat that towered somewhere over her head like a lampshade, in a blue dress with violet stripes slanting one way on the bodice and the other on the skirt, sat next to Anna, her tall, flat figure held very straight. Bending her head, she greeted Alexey Alexandrovitch with an ironical smile.

"Ah!" she said, as though surprised. "I'm so glad you're home. You're never to be seen anywhere, and I haven't seen you since Anna fell ill. I've heard all about it — your devotion. Yes, you're a remarkable husband!" she said, with a knowing, affable air, as though awarding him an order of magnanimity for his conduct toward his wife.
Alexey Alexandrovitch bowed coldly, and kissing his wife's hand, asked how she was.
"Better, I think," she said, avoiding his eyes.
"But you've a rather feverish-looking color," he said, stressing the word "feverish."
"We've been talking too much," said Betsy. "It's selfish of me, I know, and I'm going to go."
She stood up, but Anna, suddenly flushing, quickly caught at her hand.
"No — wait a minute, please. I have to tell you... no, you." She turned to Alexey Alexandrovitch, and her neck and brow flushed crimson. "I won't and can't keep anything secret from you," she said.
Alexey Alexandrovitch cracked his fingers and bowed his head.

"Betsy was just telling me that Count Vronsky wants to come here to say good-bye before his departure for Tashkend." She didn't look at her husband, and was clearly in a hurry to get the whole thing out, however hard it was for her. "I told her I couldn't receive him."
"You said, my dear, that it would depend on Alexey Alexandrovitch," Betsy corrected her.
"Oh, no — I can't receive him; and what purpose would there...." She broke off and glanced inquiringly at her husband (he was not looking at her). "In short, I don't wish it...."
Alexey Alexandrovitch stepped forward and would have taken her hand.
Her first impulse was to jerk her hand back from the damp hand with its big swollen veins that was reaching for hers, but with an obvious effort to control herself she pressed his hand.

"I'm very grateful to you for your confidence, but...." he said, feeling, with confusion and irritation, that what he could decide easily and clearly on his own, he could not discuss in front of Princess Tverskaya, who represented for him the incarnation of that brute force that would inevitably control him in the life he led in the eyes of the world, and would block him from giving way to his feeling of love and forgiveness. He broke off, looking at Princess Tverskaya.
"Well, good-bye, my darling," said Betsy, getting up. She kissed Anna and went out. Alexey Alexandrovitch saw her out.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch! I know you are a truly magnanimous man," said Betsy, stopping in the little drawing room and, with special warmth, shaking his hand again. "I'm an outsider, but I love her so much, and respect you so much, that I take the liberty of giving you advice. Receive him. Alexey Vronsky is the soul of honor, and he's leaving for Tashkend."
"Thank you, princess, for your sympathy and your advice. But the question of whom my wife can or cannot receive she must decide for herself."

He said this from habit, lifting his brows with dignity, and immediately reflected that whatever words he used, there could be no dignity in his position. And he saw as much from the suppressed, malicious, ironic smile Betsy gave him after this remark.

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch took leave of Betsy in the drawing-room and went in to his wife. She was lying down, but hearing his steps she sat up quickly into her earlier posture and looked at him in alarm. He saw she had been crying.

"I'm very grateful for your trust in me." He repeated gently in Russian the phrase he had said in French in front of Betsy, and sat down beside her. When he spoke to her in Russian, using the intimate, affectionate "thou," it was unbearably irritating to Anna. "And I'm very grateful for your decision. I too think that since he is leaving, there's no need at all for Count Vronsky to come here. However, if...."

"But I've already said so, so why repeat it?" Anna suddenly interrupted, unable to suppress her irritation. "No need at all," she thought, "for a man to come and say good-bye to the woman he loves, the woman he was ready to ruin himself for, and has ruined himself for, and who can't live without him. No need at all!" She compressed her lips, and dropped her burning eyes to his hands with their swollen veins. They were rubbing each other.
"Let's never speak of it," she added more calmly.
"I've left this question to you to decide, and I am very glad to see...." Alexey Alexandrovitch was beginning.
"That my wish coincides with your own," she finished quickly, exasperated at his speaking so slowly when she already knew everything he was going to say.
"Yes," he agreed; "and Princess Tverskaya's interference in such difficult private matters is entirely uncalled for. She, of all people...."
"I don't believe a word of what's said about her," Anna said quickly. "I know she truly cares about me."

Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed and said nothing. She fingered the tassel of her dressing-gown nervously, glancing at him with that torturing sense of physical revulsion for which she blamed herself but couldn't control. Her only wish now was to be free of his oppressive presence.
"I've just sent for the doctor," said Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"I'm perfectly well — what do I want the doctor for?"
"No, the little one is crying, and they say the nurse hasn't enough milk."

"Why didn't you let me nurse her, when I begged to? Anyway" (Alexey Alexandrovitch understood what was meant by that "anyway"), "she's a baby, and they're killing her." She rang the bell and ordered the baby brought to her. "I begged to nurse her, I wasn't allowed to, and now I'm blamed for it."
"I'm not blaming...."
"Yes you are blaming me! My God! Why didn't I die!" And she burst into sobs. "Forgive me, I'm on edge, I'm being unjust," she said, controlling herself, "but please, go away...."
"No, this can't go on," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to himself firmly as he left his wife's room.

Never before had the impossibility of his position in the eyes of the world, and his wife's hatred of him, and the whole weight of that mysterious brutal force that guided his life against his spiritual inclinations and demanded conformity with its decrees and a change in his attitude toward his wife — never had all of this been laid before him as plainly as it was that day. He saw clearly that the whole world and his wife expected something from him, but what exactly, he couldn't make out. He felt this was stirring up in him an anger that was destroying his peace of mind and all the good of what he had attained. He believed it would be better for Anna herself to break off all relations with Vronsky; but if everyone considered that out of the question, he was even ready to let those relations be renewed, as long as the children weren't disgraced, as long as he wasn't deprived of them or forced to change his position. As bad as that would be, it was still better than a rupture, which would put her in a hopeless and shameful position and strip him of everything he cared about. But he felt helpless; he knew in advance that everyone was against him, and that he wouldn't be allowed to do what now seemed to him so natural and right, but would be forced to do what was wrong, though it seemed to them the proper thing.

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Before Betsy could walk out of the drawing room, she ran into Stepan Arkadyevitch in the doorway. He had just come from Yeliseev's, where a fresh consignment of oysters had arrived.
"Ah! Princess! What a delightful coincidence!" he began. "I was on my way to see you."
"A coincidence of one minute, since I'm leaving," said Betsy, smiling and pulling on her glove.
"Don't put the glove on yet, Princess; let me kiss your hand. Of all the old fashions that have come back, this is the one I'm most grateful for." He kissed Betsy's hand. "When shall we meet again?"
"You don't deserve it," Betsy answered, still smiling.
"Oh, but I do — I deserve a great deal, because I have become a very serious person. I look after not only my own business but other people's as well," he said, with a meaningful expression.

"Oh, I'm so glad to hear that!" Betsy answered, instantly understanding that he was talking about Anna. They stepped back into the drawing room and stood in a corner. "He is killing her," Betsy said in a charged whisper. "It's impossible, impossible…."
"I'm so glad you see it that way," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, shaking his head with a serious, sympathetically pained expression. "That's exactly why I've come to Petersburg."

"The whole town is talking about it," she said. "It's an impossible position. She wastes away day by day. He doesn't understand that she's one of those women who can't play games with their feelings. There are only two ways out: either he takes her away and acts decisively, or he gives her a divorce. This is suffocating her."

"Yes, yes… exactly so…." Oblonsky said, sighing. "That's what I've come for. Not only for that, of course — I've been appointed a _Kammerherr_, and naturally I have to go through the formalities of thanks. But the main thing was settling this."
"Well, may God help you!" said Betsy.

After seeing Betsy out into the front hall, kissing her hand again above the glove at the pulse, and murmuring such improper nonsense at her that she didn't know whether to laugh or be furious, Stepan Arkadyevitch went in to his sister. He found her in tears.

Though he was bubbling with cheerfulness, Stepan Arkadyevitch immediately and quite naturally fell into the sympathetic, gently emotional tone that matched her mood. He asked how she was and how she had spent the morning.
"Very, very miserably. Today and this morning, and every day that's gone and every one that's coming," she said.
"I think you're giving in to pessimism. You have to pull yourself together, you have to face life. I know it's hard, but…."

"I've heard that women love men even for their faults," Anna burst out suddenly, "but I hate him for his virtues. I can't live with him. Do you understand? Just the sight of him has a physical effect on me — it sends me out of my mind. I can't, I can't live with him. What am I to do? I used to be unhappy and thought no one could be more unhappy, but the state I'm in now is something I could never have imagined. Can you believe that, knowing he's a good man, a fine man, that I'm not worth his little finger, I still hate him? I hate him for his generosity. And there's nothing left for me except…."
She would have said death, but Stepan Arkadyevitch wouldn't let her finish.
"You're ill and worn out," he said. "Believe me, you're exaggerating terribly. There's nothing so dreadful in it."

And Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled. In his place, no one else dealing with such despair would have risked a smile — it would have looked brutal — but in his smile there was so much sweetness and almost feminine tenderness that it didn't wound; it softened and soothed. His gentle, calming words and smiles were as soothing and softening as almond oil. And Anna soon felt it.

"No, Stiva," she said, "I'm lost — lost! Worse than lost! I can't say yet that it's all over; on the contrary, I feel it isn't over. I'm an overstretched string that has to snap. But it isn't finished yet… and the ending will be terrible."
"It doesn't matter; we just have to slacken the string, little by little. There's no situation that doesn't have a way out."
"I've thought, and thought. Only one…."
Again, from her frightened eyes, he understood that the one way out she was thinking of was death, and he wouldn't let her say it.

"Not at all," he said. "Listen to me. You can't see your own situation the way I can. Let me tell you frankly what I think." Again he smiled discreetly, his almond-oil smile. "I'll start from the beginning. You married a man twenty years older than you. You married him without love, not knowing what love was. That was a mistake — let's grant it."
"A terrible mistake!" said Anna.

"But, I repeat, it's a done thing. Then you had, let's say, the misfortune of loving a man who wasn't your husband. That was a misfortune; but that, too, is a done thing. And your husband knew it and forgave it." He paused at each sentence, expecting her to object, but she said nothing. "That's how matters stand. Now the question is: can you go on living with your husband? Do you want to? Does he want to?"
"I don't know — I don't know anything."
"But you just said yourself that you can't stand him."
"No, I didn't say that. I take it back. I can't tell, I don't know anything about it."
"Yes, but let me…."
"You can't understand. I feel as though I'm falling head down into some pit, and I shouldn't try to save myself. And I can't…."
"Never mind, we'll slide something underneath and pull you out. I understand you — I understand that you can't bring yourself to put your wishes and feelings into words."
"There's nothing, nothing I want… except for it all to be over."

"But he sees that and knows it. And do you suppose it weighs on him any less than on you? You're wretched, he's wretched — and what good comes of it? Whereas a divorce would solve the whole thing." With some effort Stepan Arkadyevitch came out with his central idea, and looked at her meaningfully.

She said nothing and shook her cropped head, refusing. But from the look on her face, which suddenly brightened into its old beauty, he saw that the only reason she wasn't wanting this was that it struck her as a happiness she could never have.

"I'm terribly sorry for you! And how happy I'd be if I could fix things!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, smiling more boldly. "Don't say anything, don't say a word! May God only grant that I can speak the way I feel. I'm going to him."
Anna looked at him with dreamy, shining eyes and said nothing.

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch, with the same faintly solemn manner he used to wear when taking the chair at his board meetings, walked into Alexey Alexandrovitch's room. Alexey Alexandrovitch was pacing about with his hands behind his back, thinking about the very thing Stepan Arkadyevitch had just been discussing with his wife.

"I'm not interrupting?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who was suddenly conscious of an embarrassment unusual for him at the sight of his brother-in-law. To cover it he pulled out a cigarette case he had just bought, one that opened in a new way, and sniffed the leather before taking out a cigarette.
"No. Is there something you want?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked without warmth.
"Yes, I wished… I wanted… yes, I wanted to talk with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, startled to find himself feeling an unfamiliar shyness.
The feeling was so unexpected and so strange that he refused to recognize it as the voice of conscience telling him that what he was about to do was wrong.
Stepan Arkadyevitch made an effort and pushed past the timidity that had come over him.
"I hope you believe in my love for my sister and in my sincere affection and respect for you," he said, reddening.
Alexey Alexandrovitch stood motionless and said nothing, but his face struck Stepan Arkadyevitch with its expression of unresisting sacrifice.
"I intended… I wanted to have a little talk with you about my sister and about your situation together," he said, still wrestling with that unaccustomed constraint.
