Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled sadly, looked at his brother-in-law, and without answering walked over to the table, picked up an unfinished letter, and handed it to him.

"I think of nothing else. And here — this is what I had started to write, because I thought I could say it better in a letter, and because my presence irritates her," he said as he gave him the letter.
Stepan Arkadyevitch took it, glanced with incredulous surprise at the dull eyes fixed steadily on him, and began to read.

"I see that my presence is a burden to you. Painful as it is for me to believe it, I see that it is so and that it cannot be otherwise. I do not blame you, and God is my witness that, when I saw you during your illness, I resolved with my whole heart to forget all that had passed between us and to begin a new life. I do not regret, and never will regret, what I did; but I have wanted one thing — your good, the good of your soul — and now I see that I have failed to achieve it. Tell me yourself what will give you true happiness and peace of soul. I put myself entirely in your hands, and I trust your sense of what is right."

Stepan Arkadyevitch handed back the letter, and with the same surprise kept staring at his brother-in-law, not knowing what to say. The silence was so awkward for both of them that Stepan Arkadyevitch's lips began to twitch nervously as he went on gazing wordlessly at Karenin's face.
"That's what I wanted to say to her," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, turning away.
"Yes, yes…." said Stepan Arkadyevitch, unable to answer because of the tears choking him.
"Yes, yes, I understand you," he finally got out.
"I want to know what she would like," said Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"I'm afraid she doesn't understand her own position. She is not the right judge," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, recovering. "She is crushed — simply crushed by your generosity. If she read this letter, she wouldn't be able to say a word; she would only hang her head still lower."
"Yes, but what is to be done in that case? How can I explain — how find out what she wants?"
"If you'll allow me to give my opinion, I think it falls to you to spell out directly the steps you consider necessary to put an end to the situation."
"So you think it has to be ended?" Alexey Alexandrovitch interrupted him. "But how?" he added, lifting his hands before his eyes in a gesture not usual with him. "I see no way out."

"There is some way out of every situation," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, standing up and growing more cheerful. "There was a time when you considered breaking it off…. If you are now convinced that you cannot make each other happy…."
"Happiness can be defined in different ways. But suppose I agree to everything, that I want nothing — what way out of our situation is there then?"

"If you care to hear my opinion," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, with the same soothing, almond-oil smile he had used with Anna. His friendly smile was so winning that Alexey Alexandrovitch, conscious of his own weakness and unconsciously swayed by it, was ready to believe whatever Stepan Arkadyevitch was about to tell him.

"She will never say it. But there is one thing possible, one thing she might wish for," he went on, "and that is the end of your relationship and of all the memories tied to it. The way I see it, in your position what's needed is a new footing toward each other. And that can only stand on a foundation of freedom on both sides."
"Divorce," Alexey Alexandrovitch interrupted, in a tone of distaste.

"Yes, I suppose divorce — yes, divorce," Stepan Arkadyevitch repeated, reddening. "From every angle that is the most reasonable course for married people who find themselves in your situation. What else can be done if married people discover that life together has become impossible? That can always happen."
Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed heavily and closed his eyes.
"There's only one point to consider: does either of you want to form new ties? If not, the matter is very simple," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, his constraint slipping further away.

Alexey Alexandrovitch, scowling with emotion, muttered something to himself and gave no answer. What seemed so simple to Stepan Arkadyevitch, Alexey Alexandrovitch had thought through a thousand times. And so far from being simple, it all looked utterly impossible to him. Divorce, the details of which he knew by now, struck him as out of the question, because his sense of his own dignity and his respect for religion would not let him take on himself a fictitious accusation of adultery — still less let his wife, whom he had forgiven and still loved, be caught in the act and publicly disgraced. Divorce seemed impossible to him on other, weightier grounds as well.

What would become of his son in the event of a divorce? Leaving him with his mother was out of the question. The divorced mother would have her own illegitimate family, in which his position as a stepson and his upbringing would not be good. Keep him with himself? He knew that would be an act of revenge on his part, and he did not want that. But beyond all this, what made divorce most impossible of all to Alexey Alexandrovitch was that by agreeing to it he would be completely destroying Anna. Darya Alexandrovna's words in Moscow — that in deciding on a divorce he was thinking of himself, and not considering that by doing so he would be ruining her past saving — had sunk deep into him. And connecting that with his forgiveness of her and his devotion to the children, he understood it now in his own way. To consent to a divorce, to give her her freedom, meant in his mind to take from himself the last thing tying him to life — the children whom he loved; and to take from her the last support that held her on the path of right, pushing her down to her ruin. If she were divorced, he knew she would join her life to Vronsky's, and their union would be an unlawful, criminal one, since by the interpretation of church law a wife cannot marry while her husband is living. "She'll join him, and in a year or two he'll throw her over, or she'll form a new attachment," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought. "And I, by consenting to an unlawful divorce, will be to blame for her ruin." He had thought it all through hundreds of times, and was convinced that divorce was not at all simple, as Stepan Arkadyevitch had said, but utterly impossible. He didn't believe a single word Stepan Arkadyevitch was saying to him; to every word he had a thousand objections to raise, yet he kept listening, feeling that the words were the voice of that crude, overpowering force that ruled his life and to which he would have to submit.
"The only question is on what terms you would agree to give her a divorce. She wants nothing, she doesn't dare ask you for anything — she leaves it all to your generosity."

"My God, my God! Why?" thought Alexey Alexandrovitch, remembering the details of divorce proceedings in which the husband took the blame on himself, and with exactly the same gesture Vronsky had once made, he hid his face in his hands for shame.
"You're upset, I understand. But if you think it over…."
"Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; and if any man take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also," thought Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"Yes, yes!" he cried in a shrill voice. "I'll take the disgrace on myself, I'll even give up my son, but… wouldn't it be better to leave it all alone? Still, do as you like…."

And turning away so his brother-in-law could not see him, he sat down on a chair by the window. There was bitterness in his heart, there was shame, but along with the bitterness and shame he felt a joy and a thrill at the height of his own meekness.
Stepan Arkadyevitch was touched. He stayed silent for a while.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch, believe me, she values your generosity," he said. "But it seems this was the will of God," he added, and as soon as he had said it he felt how foolish the remark was and barely kept from smiling at his own foolishness.
Alexey Alexandrovitch would have answered something, but tears stopped him.
"This is an unhappy fate, and one must accept it as such. I accept the calamity as a done thing and I'm doing what I can to help both her and you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

When he left his brother-in-law's room he was moved, but that didn't prevent him from being pleased that he had brought the business to a satisfactory close, for he was certain that Alexey Alexandrovitch would not go back on his words. To this satisfaction was added the fact that an idea had just struck him for a riddle turning on his successful achievement — one he would ask his wife and his closest friends once the affair was finished. He turned the riddle over in two or three different forms. "But I'll polish it better than that," he said to himself with a smile.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Vronsky's wound had been a dangerous one, though it had not touched the heart, and for several days he had hung between life and death. The first time he was able to speak, Varya, his brother's wife, was alone with him in the room.
"Varya," he said, looking at her sternly, "I shot myself by accident. And please — never mention it, and tell everyone the same. Otherwise it's just absurd."
Without answering, Varya bent over him and gazed into his face with a delighted smile. His eyes were clear, not feverish, but their expression was stern.
"Thank God!" she said. "You're not in pain?"
"A little, here." He pointed to his chest.
"Then let me change your dressings."
In silence, his broad jaws clenched, he watched her while she bandaged him. When she had finished he said:
"I'm not delirious. Please see to it that nobody says I shot myself on purpose."
"No one is saying it. Only — I hope you won't shoot yourself by accident again," she said, with a questioning smile.
"Of course I won't, but it would have been better…."
And he gave a grim smile.

Despite these words and that smile, which frightened Varya, once the inflammation passed and he started to recover, he felt that he was completely free of one part of his misery. Through what he had done he had, as it were, washed away the shame and humiliation he had been carrying before. He could now think calmly about Alexey Alexandrovitch. He acknowledged all the man's generosity, but he no longer felt humiliated by it. Besides, he had stepped back into the familiar track of his life. He saw that he could meet people's eyes again without shame, and could live by his own habits. The one thing he could not pull out of his heart, though he never stopped struggling with it, was the regret — close to despair — that he had lost her forever. That now, having atoned for his sin against the husband, he was obliged to give her up and never again come between her and her repentant husband, he had firmly decided in his heart; but he could not tear out of his heart the regret over losing her love, could not wipe from his memory those moments of happiness he had so little valued at the time, and which now haunted him in all their charm.

Serpuhovskoy had arranged a posting for him to Tashkent, and Vronsky accepted the offer without a moment's hesitation. But the closer the departure date came, the more bitter the sacrifice he was making to what he considered his duty.
His wound healed, and he was driving around making preparations to leave for Tashkent.

"To see her once, and then to bury myself, to die," he thought, and as he was making his farewell calls he said as much to Betsy. With that commission, Betsy went to Anna and came back with a refusal.
"So much the better," Vronsky thought when he got the news. "It was a weakness, and it would have shattered what strength I have left."

The next morning Betsy came to him herself, and announced that she had heard from Oblonsky, as a certainty, that Alexey Alexandrovitch had agreed to a divorce, and that Vronsky could therefore see Anna.

Without even bothering to see Betsy out of his apartment, forgetting all his resolutions, without asking when he could see Anna or where her husband was, Vronsky drove straight to the Karenins'. He ran up the stairs seeing no one and nothing, and with a quick stride — almost breaking into a run — he went into her room. And without stopping to see whether anyone else was there, he threw his arms around her and began to cover her face, her hands, and her neck with kisses.

Anna had been preparing herself for this meeting, had thought through what she would say to him, but she didn't get to say any of it; his passion took her over. She tried to calm him, to calm herself, but it was too late. His feeling caught her up. Her lips were trembling so hard that for a long while she could say nothing.
"Yes, you've conquered me, and I am yours," she finally said, pressing his hands to her breast.
"It had to be this way," he said. "As long as we live, it must be so. I know that now."
"That's true," she said, growing whiter and whiter, holding his head close. "Still, there's something dreadful about it, after everything that has happened."

"It will all pass, it will all pass; we'll be so happy. Our love, if it could be stronger, will be made stronger by there being something dreadful in it," he said, lifting his head and showing his strong teeth in a smile.
And she couldn't help responding with a smile — not to his words, but to the love in his eyes. She took his hand and stroked her chilled cheeks and her cropped hair with it.
"I don't recognize you with this short hair. You've grown so pretty. Like a boy. But how pale you are!"
"Yes, I'm very weak," she said, smiling. And her lips began to tremble again.
"We'll go to Italy; you'll get your strength back," he said.
"Can it really be that we'll be like husband and wife, alone — with you and your family?" she said, looking closely into his eyes.
"What seems strange to me is that it could ever have been any other way."

"Stiva says that _he_ has agreed to everything, but I can't accept _his_ generosity," she said, gazing dreamily past Vronsky's face. "I don't want a divorce; nothing matters to me now. The only thing is, I don't know what he'll decide about Seryozha."
He could not understand how, at this moment of their reunion, she could remember and think about her son and a divorce. What did any of it matter?
"Don't talk about that, don't think about it," he said, turning her hand in his and trying to pull her attention back to him; but still she would not look at him.
"Oh, why didn't I die? It would have been better," she said, and silent tears ran down both her cheeks; but she tried to smile so as not to hurt him.

To turn down the flattering and risky posting to Tashkent would, until then, have struck Vronsky as disgraceful and impossible. But now, without a moment's thought, he turned it down, and, observing displeasure in the highest quarters at this step, he immediately retired from the army.

A month later Alexey Alexandrovitch was left alone with his son in his Petersburg house, while Anna and Vronsky had gone abroad — not having obtained a divorce, but having completely given up the idea of one.
PART FIVE

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Princess Shtcherbatskaya thought it was out of the question for the wedding to take place before Lent, only five weeks off, since not half the trousseau could possibly be ready in time. But she had to agree with Levin that putting it off until after Lent would be cutting it too late: an old aunt of Prince Shtcherbatsky's was seriously ill and might die, in which case mourning would push the wedding back even further. And so, deciding to split the trousseau into two parts — a larger one and a smaller one — the princess agreed to a wedding before Lent. She determined to have the smaller part of the trousseau ready now and the larger part made later, and she was very annoyed with Levin because he couldn't give her a serious answer to whether he approved of this arrangement or not. The arrangement suited all the better because, right after the wedding, the young couple were to leave for the country, where the more important part of the trousseau would not be needed.

Levin remained in the same dazed state, in which it seemed to him that he and his happiness were the chief and only goal of all existence, and that he no longer needed to think about anything or worry about anything — everything was being done and would be done for him by others. He had no plans or aims for the future; he left it to others to arrange, knowing that everything would turn out wonderfully. His brother Sergey Ivanovitch, Stepan Arkadyevitch, and the princess guided him in what he had to do. All he did was agree with whatever was suggested. His brother raised money for him, the princess advised him to leave Moscow after the wedding, Stepan Arkadyevitch advised him to go abroad. He agreed to everything. "Do whatever you like, if it amuses you. I'm happy, and my happiness can't be any greater or any less for anything you do," he thought. When he told Kitty about Stepan Arkadyevitch's idea of going abroad, he was greatly surprised that she didn't agree to it and had quite definite preferences of her own about their future. She knew that Levin had work he loved in the country. She did not, as he could see, understand that work, and she didn't even care to understand it. But that didn't keep her from regarding it as very important. And then she knew that their home would be in the country, and she wanted to go there — not abroad, where she wasn't going to live, but to the place where their home would be. This clearly stated preference astonished Levin. But since he didn't care either way, he immediately asked Stepan Arkadyevitch — almost as if it were his obligation — to go down to the country and arrange everything there as well as he could, with that taste of his that he had so much of.
"By the way," Stepan Arkadyevitch said to him one day after coming back from the country, where he had got everything ready for the young couple's arrival, "do you have a certificate of confession?"
"No. Why?"
"You can't get married without one."
"_Aïe, aïe, aïe!_" cried Levin. "It must be nine years since I've taken the sacrament! I never thought of it."
"You're a fine one!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, laughing. "And you call me a Nihilist! But this won't do, you know. You have to take the sacrament."
"When? Only four days are left now."

Stepan Arkadyevitch arranged this too, and Levin had to go to confession. For Levin, as for any unbeliever who respects other people's beliefs, taking part in any church ceremony was extremely disagreeable. At this moment, in his softened state, sensitive to everything, this inevitable act of hypocrisy was not merely painful to Levin — it seemed impossible. Now, in the height of his glory, his fullest flowering, he would have to be either a liar or a mocker. He felt incapable of being either. But although he repeatedly pestered Stepan Arkadyevitch about the possibility of getting a certificate without actually taking communion, Stepan Arkadyevitch insisted that there was no way around it.
"Besides, what does it cost you — two days? And he's a very nice, clever old fellow. He'll pull the tooth out for you so gently you won't even notice."
Standing through the first litany, Levin tried to bring back in himself his youthful memories of the intense religious feeling he had gone through between the ages of sixteen and seventeen.

But he was instantly convinced that this was completely impossible for him. He tried to look at it all as an empty custom with no meaning, like the custom of paying social calls. But he felt he couldn't do that either. Levin found himself, like most of his contemporaries, in the vaguest position with regard to religion. He couldn't believe, and at the same time he had no firm conviction that it was all wrong. And so, unable to believe in the importance of what he was doing, and unable to look on it indifferently as an empty formality, throughout the whole preparation for the sacrament he felt uncomfortable and ashamed at doing what he didn't himself understand — what, as an inner voice told him, was therefore false and wrong.

During the service he would first listen to the prayers, trying to attach some meaning to them that wasn't at odds with his own views; then, feeling he couldn't understand them and would have to condemn them, he tried not to listen and to attend instead to the thoughts, observations, and memories that drifted through his mind with extreme vividness during this idle stretch of standing in church.

He had stood through the litany, the evening service, and the midnight service, and the next day he got up earlier than usual and, without taking tea, went to the church at eight in the morning for the morning service and his confession.

There was no one in the church except a beggar soldier, two old women, and the church staff. A young deacon, his long back showing in two distinct halves through his thin undercassock, met him and, going at once to a little table by the wall, read the exhortation. During the reading, especially at the frequent rapid repetition of the words "Lord, have mercy on us!" which rang back from the echo, Levin felt that his thoughts were shut and sealed away, and that they mustn't be touched or disturbed now, or chaos would follow. So, standing behind the deacon, he went on thinking about his own affairs, neither listening to nor examining what was being said. "It's wonderful what expression there is in her hand," he thought, remembering how they had been sitting at a corner table the day before. They had nothing to talk about, as was almost always the case at this point, and laying her hand on the table she had kept opening and shutting it, laughing as she watched her own movement. He remembered how he had kissed it and then traced the lines on her pink palm. "Have mercy on us again!" Levin thought, crossing himself, bowing, and watching the supple flex of the deacon's back as he bowed in front of him. "She took my hand then and traced the lines. 'You have a splendid hand,' she said." And he looked at his own hand and at the deacon's short one. "Yes, it'll be over soon," he thought. "No, it seems to be starting again," he thought, listening to the prayers. "No, it's just ending — there he is bowing to the ground. That's always the end."

The deacon's hand in its plush cuff unobtrusively accepted a three-rouble note, and he said he would enter it in the register; then, his new boots creaking jauntily across the flagstones of the empty church, he went off to the altar. A moment later he peeped out from behind it and beckoned to Levin. Thoughts, until then locked up, began to stir in Levin's head, but he hurried to push them away. "It'll come out right somehow," he thought, and walked toward the altar rails. He climbed the steps and, turning to the right, saw the priest. The priest, a small old man with a thin grizzled beard and tired, kindly eyes, was standing at the altar rails turning the pages of a missal. With a slight bow to Levin he began at once to read prayers in the formal voice. When he had finished them, he bowed to the ground and turned to face Levin.

"Christ is present here unseen, receiving your confession," he said, pointing to the crucifix. "Do you believe in all the doctrines of the Holy Apostolic Church?" the priest went on, looking away from Levin's face and folding his hands under his stole.
"I have doubted, I doubt everything," Levin said in a voice that grated on himself, and he stopped.
The priest waited a few seconds to see if he would add anything, then, closing his eyes, he said rapidly, with a broad Vladimir accent:
"Doubt is natural to the weakness of mankind, but we must pray that God in His mercy will strengthen us. What are your particular sins?" he added without a pause, as though anxious not to lose time.
"My chief sin is doubt. I have doubts about everything, and most of the time I'm in doubt."
"Doubt is natural to the weakness of mankind," the priest repeated, using the same words. "What is it you doubt most of all?"

"I doubt everything. I sometimes even have doubts about the existence of God," Levin couldn't help saying, and he was horrified at the impropriety of his own words. But Levin's words didn't seem to make much impression on the priest.
"What sort of doubt can there be of the existence of God?" he said quickly, with a barely perceptible smile.
Levin said nothing.

"How can you doubt the Creator when you look at His creation?" the priest went on in his rapid customary patter. "Who has decked the heavens with their lights? Who has clothed the earth in its beauty? How explain it without a Creator?" he said, looking inquiringly at Levin.
Levin felt it would be improper to get into a metaphysical discussion with the priest, so he confined himself to a direct answer to the question.
"I don't know," he said.
"You don't know! Then how can you doubt that God created everything?" the priest said, with good-humored bewilderment.
"I don't understand any of it," Levin said, blushing, feeling that his words were silly and could only be silly in such a setting.

"Pray to God and ask Him. Even the holy fathers had doubts and prayed to God to strengthen their faith. The devil has great power, and we must resist him. Pray to God, beseech Him. Pray to God," he repeated hurriedly.
The priest paused for a while, as if thinking.
"You're about, I hear, to marry the daughter of my parishioner and son in the spirit, Prince Shtcherbatsky?" he resumed, with a smile. "A fine young lady."
"Yes," Levin answered, blushing for the priest. "What does he want to ask me about that at confession for?" he thought.
And as if in answer to his thought, the priest said:

"You are about to enter into holy matrimony, and God may bless you with children. Well — what sort of upbringing can you give your little ones if you don't overcome the temptation of the devil that draws you into unbelief?" he said, with gentle reproach. "If you love your child like a good father, you won't only want wealth, luxury, and honor for your baby; you'll be anxious for his salvation, for his spiritual enlightenment by the light of truth. Yes? What answer will you give him when the innocent child asks you: 'Papa! Who made everything that enchants me in this world — the earth, the waters, the sun, the flowers, the grasses?' Can you say to him: 'I don't know'? You cannot but know, since the Lord God in His infinite mercy has revealed it to us. Or your child will ask you: 'What awaits me in the life beyond the tomb?' What will you say to him when you know nothing? Will you leave him to the temptations of the world and the devil? That isn't right," he said, and stopped, putting his head on one side and looking at Levin with his kind, gentle eyes.

Levin made no answer this time — not because he didn't want to argue with the priest, but because, up to now, no one had ever put such questions to him, and when his children did, there would be time enough then to think about how to answer them.

"You are entering a stage of life," the priest continued, "where you must choose your path and stick to it. Pray to God, that He in His mercy may help you and have mercy on you!" he concluded. "Our Lord and God Jesus Christ, in the abundance and riches of His loving-kindness, forgives this child…." And, finishing the prayer of absolution, the priest blessed him and dismissed him.

Walking home that day, Levin had a wonderful sense of relief that the awkward business was over and that he had got through it without having to lie. Beyond that, there was a vague memory that what the kind, nice old fellow had said hadn't been nearly as stupid as he had thought at first, and that there was something in it that needed to be cleared up.

"Not now, of course," Levin thought, "but at some point later on." Levin felt more strongly than ever that there was something unclear and unclean in his soul, and that, with regard to religion, he was in the same position he could see so clearly and dislike so much in others, and for which he blamed his friend Sviazhsky.

Levin spent that evening with his betrothed at Dolly's, and was in very high spirits. To describe to Stepan Arkadyevitch the state of excitement he was in, he said he felt as happy as a dog being trained to jump through a hoop, who, having finally caught the idea and done what was asked of it, whines and wags its tail and leaps up onto tables and windows in its delight.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: On the wedding day, following the Russian custom (and the princess and Darya Alexandrovna insisted on strictly following all the customs), Levin did not see his betrothed, and dined at his hotel with three bachelor friends who happened to come together in his rooms. These were Sergey Ivanovitch; Katavasov, a friend from university now a professor of natural science, whom Levin had run into on the street and pulled home with him; and Tchirikov, his best man, a Moscow conciliation-board judge and Levin's companion in his bear hunts. The dinner was a very cheerful one. Sergey Ivanovitch was in his best humor and very much enjoyed Katavasov's eccentricity. Katavasov, feeling that his eccentricity was appreciated and understood, made the most of it. Tchirikov gave any conversation a lively, good-natured support.

"See, now," said Katavasov, drawling his words in a habit picked up in the lecture hall, "what a capable fellow our friend Konstantin Dmitrievitch was. I'm not speaking of present company, since he's absent. When he left the university he was fond of science, took an interest in humanity; now half his abilities are devoted to deceiving himself, and the other half to justifying the deceit."
"I've never met a more determined enemy of marriage than you," said Sergey Ivanovitch.

"Oh no, I'm no enemy of marriage. I'm in favor of the division of labor. People who can't do anything else ought to raise children, while the rest work for their happiness and enlightenment. That's how I look at it. Mixing up two trades is the amateur's mistake; I'm not one of them."
"How happy I'll be on the day I hear that you've fallen in love!" said Levin. "Please invite me to the wedding."
"I'm in love now."
"Yes — with a cuttlefish! You know," Levin said, turning to his brother, "Mihail Semyonovitch is writing a study on the digestive organs of the…."
"Now, now, don't muddle it. It doesn't really matter what about. The fact is, I genuinely do love cuttlefish."
"But that's no reason you can't love your wife."
"The cuttlefish doesn't get in the way. The wife does."
"Why?"
"Oh, you'll see! You care about farming, about hunting — well, you'd better watch out!"
"Arhip was here today; he said there were a lot of elk in Prudno, and two bears," said Tchirikov.
"Well, you'll have to go get them without me."
"Ah, that's the truth," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "And you can say goodbye to bear hunting from now on — your wife won't allow it!"
Levin smiled. The picture of his wife not letting him go was so pleasant that he was ready to give up the pleasure of laying eyes on bears forever.
"Still, it's a pity those two bears get taken without you. Remember last time at Hapilovo? That was a wonderful hunt!" said Tchirikov.
Levin hadn't the heart to disabuse him of the idea that there could be anything delightful apart from her, and so said nothing.
"There's some sense to this custom of saying goodbye to bachelor life," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "However happy you may be, you must miss your freedom."
"And admit you have a feeling of wanting to jump out the window, like Gogol's bridegroom?"
"Of course there is, but no one admits it," said Katavasov, and broke into loud laughter.

"Well, the window's open. Let's set off this instant for Tver! There's a big she-bear there; you can walk right up to the lair. Honestly, let's catch the five o'clock! And let them here do what they please," said Tchirikov, smiling.
"Well, on my honor," Levin said with a smile, "I can't find in myself that regret for my freedom."
"Yes, there's such a chaos in your heart just now that you can't find anything in there," Katavasov said. "Wait until you've put it back in order a bit — then you'll find it!"

"No — if it were there, I'd feel a little, apart from my feeling" (he couldn't say love in front of them) "and my happiness, some regret at losing my freedom…. On the contrary, I'm glad about the very loss of my freedom."

"Hopeless! It's a hopeless case!" Katavasov said. "Well, let's drink to his recovery — or wish that one hundredth of his dreams comes true. Even that would be happiness such as the earth has never seen!"
Soon after dinner the guests left to get dressed in time for the wedding.

Left alone, and going back over the conversation of these bachelor friends, Levin asked himself: did he in his heart feel that regret for his freedom they had spoken of? He smiled at the question. "Freedom! What is freedom for? Happiness is only in loving and wanting what she wants, thinking her thoughts — that is, no freedom at all. That's happiness!"

"But do I know her ideas, her wishes, her feelings?" some voice suddenly whispered. The smile faded from his face, and he grew thoughtful. Suddenly a strange feeling came over him. A dread, a doubt — doubt of everything — came down on him.

"What if she doesn't love me? What if she's marrying me just to be married? What if she herself doesn't see what she's doing?" he asked himself. "She may come to her senses, and only when the ceremony is under way realize that she doesn't and can't love me." And strange, very ugly thoughts about her began coming to him. He was jealous of Vronsky, the way he had been a year ago, as if the evening he had seen her with Vronsky were yesterday. He suspected she had not told him everything.

He jumped up quickly. "No, this can't go on!" he said to himself in despair. "I'll go to her; I'll ask her; I'll say one last time: we are still free, hadn't we better stay so? Anything is better than endless misery, disgrace, unfaithfulness!" With despair in his heart, and bitter anger against everyone — against himself, against her — he left the hotel and drove to her house.

He found her in one of the back rooms. She was sitting on a chest, sorting through heaps of dresses of different colors spread over the backs of chairs and on the floor, working things out with her maid.

"Ah!" she cried when she saw him, beaming with joy. "Kostya! Konstantin Dmitrievitch!" (These last few days she had been using both names almost interchangeably.) "I didn't expect you! I'm going through my wardrobe to see what goes to whom…."
"Oh! that's nice," he said gloomily, with a look at the maid.

"You can go, Dunyasha, I'll call you in a moment," said Kitty. "Kostya, what's the matter?" she asked, settling firmly on the familiar name as soon as the maid was out. She had noticed his strange face — agitated and dark — and a panic took hold of her.

"Kitty! I'm in torment. I can't bear it alone," he said with despair in his voice, standing before her and looking imploringly into her eyes. He could see already from her loving, honest face that nothing could come of what he had meant to say, but he wanted her to reassure him all the same. "I've come to say that there's still time. We can stop all this and put it right."
"What? I don't understand. What is the matter?"

"What I've said a thousand times, and can't help thinking… that I'm not worthy of you. You couldn't have agreed to marry me. Think a little. You've made a mistake. Think it through carefully. You can't love me…. If… better tell me," he said, not looking at her. "I'll be miserable. Let people say what they want; anything's better than misery…. Far better now, while there's still time…."
"I don't understand," she said, panic-stricken. "You mean you want to call it off… you don't want to?"
"Yes, if you don't love me."

"You're out of your mind!" she cried, going crimson with exasperation. But his face was so pitiful that she held back her anger and, tossing some clothes off an armchair, she sat down next to him. "What are you thinking? Tell me everything."
"I'm thinking you can't love me. What is there for you to love me for?"
"My God! What am I to do?…" she said, and burst into tears.
"Oh! What have I done?" he cried, and dropping to his knees in front of her, he started kissing her hands.

When the princess came into the room five minutes later, she found them completely reconciled. Kitty had not only assured him that she loved him; she had gone so far — in answer to his question, what she loved him for — as to spell it out. She told him she loved him because she understood him through and through, because she knew what he would like, and because everything he liked was good. And this struck him as perfectly clear. When the princess came in, they were sitting side by side on the chest, sorting dresses and arguing because Kitty wanted to give Dunyasha the brown dress she had been wearing when Levin proposed, while he insisted that that dress must never be given away — Dunyasha must have the blue one.
"How can you not see it? She's a brunette, and it won't suit her…. I've worked it all out."

Hearing what he had come for, the princess was half jokingly, half seriously cross with him and sent him home to get dressed, and not to interfere with Kitty's hair, since Charles the hairdresser was about to arrive.
"As it is, she's been eating nothing lately and is losing her looks, and then you come and upset her with your nonsense," she said to him. "Off you go, my dear!"

Guilty and shamefaced but calmed, Levin went back to his hotel. His brother, Darya Alexandrovna, and Stepan Arkadyevitch, all in formal dress, were waiting to bless him with the holy picture. There was no time to lose. Darya Alexandrovna still had to drive home and fetch her curled and pomaded son, who was to carry the holy pictures behind the bride. Then one carriage had to be sent for the best man, and another, which would take Sergey Ivanovitch, would have to be sent back…. Altogether there was a great deal of complicated logistics to think through and sort out. One thing was certain: there must be no delay, since it was already half past six.

Nothing special happened during the ceremony of benediction with the holy picture. Stepan Arkadyevitch stood beside his wife in a comically solemn pose, took the holy picture, and, telling Levin to bow to the ground, blessed him with his kind, slightly ironic smile and kissed him three times; Darya Alexandrovna did the same and was instantly in a hurry to be off, plunging again into the tangled question of which carriage was going where.
"Come, I'll tell you how we'll manage: you take our carriage to go fetch him, and Sergey Ivanovitch — if he'll be so good — will go on ahead and send his carriage back."
"Of course; I'll be delighted to."
"We'll come on right after with him. Has your luggage gone?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Yes," Levin answered, and he told Kouzma to lay out his clothes for him to dress.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: A crowd, most of them women, was pressing around the church, lit up for the wedding. Those who hadn't managed to get in through the main entrance were jostling at the windows, pushing, quarreling, and peering through the gratings.

More than twenty carriages had already been lined up along the street by the police. A police officer, paying no attention to the cold, stood at the entrance in his splendid uniform. More carriages kept driving up, and ladies in flowers, holding up their trains, and men taking off their helmets or black hats kept walking into the church. Inside the church, both chandeliers were already lit, along with all the candles before the holy pictures. The gilt against the red ground of the icon stand, the gilt relief on the icons themselves, the silver of the chandeliers and candlesticks, the stones of the floor, the rugs, the banners above in the choir, the steps of the altar, the old blackened books, and the cassocks and surplices — all of it was bathed in light. On the right side of the warm church, in the crowd of frock coats and white ties, uniforms and broadcloth, velvet, satin, hair, flowers, bare shoulders and arms and long gloves, there was a quiet but lively conversation that echoed strangely in the high dome. Every time the door creaked open, the talk in the crowd died, and everyone looked round, expecting to see the bride and groom come in. But the door had been opened more than ten times, and each time it was either a late guest or guests who joined the circle of the invited on the right, or some spectator who had slipped past or won over the police officer and joined the crowd of outsiders on the left. Both the guests and the outside public had by now gone through all the phases of waiting.

At first they assumed the bride and groom would arrive any moment and gave no importance to their being late. Then they began glancing toward the door more and more often and started wondering whether something might have happened. Then the long wait grew positively uncomfortable, and the relatives and guests tried to look as if they weren't thinking about the bridegroom but were absorbed in conversation.

The head deacon, as if to remind everyone how valuable his time was, kept coughing impatiently, rattling the windowpanes in their frames. In the choir, the bored singers could be heard trying their voices and blowing their noses. The priest kept sending first the beadle and then the deacon to find out whether the bridegroom had come; more and more frequently he went himself, in his lilac vestment and embroidered sash, to the side door to look out for the bridegroom. Finally one of the ladies glanced at her watch and said, "It really is strange, though!" — and then all the guests grew uneasy and started loudly voicing their wonder and dissatisfaction. One of the bridegroom's groomsmen went off to find out what had happened. Meanwhile Kitty had long since been completely ready, and in her white dress, long veil, and wreath of orange blossoms, she was standing in the drawing room of the Shtcherbatskys' house with her sister, Madame Lvova, who was her bridal mother. She was looking out the window, having been anxiously waiting for half an hour to hear from the best man that her bridegroom was at the church.

Levin, meanwhile, in his trousers but without coat or waistcoat, was pacing back and forth in his hotel room, constantly poking his head out the door and looking up and down the corridor. But the person he was watching for was nowhere in the corridor, and he came back in despair, throwing up his hands and turning to Stepan Arkadyevitch, who was calmly smoking.
"Was ever a man in a more ridiculous spot?" he said.
"Yes, it's silly," Stepan Arkadyevitch agreed, smiling soothingly. "But don't worry — it'll be here any minute."

"No, what is to be done!" Levin said, with smothered fury. "And these stupid open waistcoats! Out of the question!" he said, looking at the crumpled front of his shirt. "And what if my things have already been sent to the railway station!" he roared in desperation.
"Then you'll have to put on mine."
"I should have done that ages ago, if at all."
"It's not nice to look ridiculous…. Wait a bit! It'll _come round_."
What had happened was that when Levin had called for his evening clothes, Kouzma, his old servant, had brought him the coat, the waistcoat, and everything that was needed.
"But the shirt!" cried Levin.
"You've got a shirt on," Kouzma answered with a placid smile.

Kouzma had not thought of leaving out a clean shirt, and when he was told to pack everything up and send it over to the Shtcherbatskys', from whose house the newlyweds were to set out that same evening, he had done so — packing everything except the evening suit. The shirt Levin had worn since morning was crumpled and out of the question with the fashionable open waistcoat. It was too far to send to the Shtcherbatskys'. They sent out to buy a shirt. The servant came back: everything was shut — it was Sunday. They sent to Stepan Arkadyevitch's and brought a shirt back — it was impossibly wide and short. They sent finally to the Shtcherbatskys' to unpack the things. The bridegroom was being waited for at the church while he was pacing his room like a wild beast in a cage, peering out into the corridor, and recalling with horror and despair the absurd things he had said to Kitty and what she might be thinking now.
At last the guilty Kouzma flew panting into the room with the shirt.
"Just in time. They were lifting it into the van," said Kouzma.
Three minutes later Levin was racing down the corridor at full speed, not daring to look at his watch for fear of making his suffering worse.
"You won't help matters this way," said Stepan Arkadyevitch with a smile, hurrying after him more leisurely. "It will come round, it will come round… I tell you."

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: "They've come!" "Here he is!" "Which one?" "Pretty young, isn't he?" "Why, my dear, she looks half dead!" — that was the running commentary in the crowd as Levin met his bride in the entryway and walked with her into the church.
Stepan Arkadyevitch explained the reason for the delay to his wife, and the guests passed it down the line in smiling whispers. Levin saw nothing and no one — his eyes never left his bride.

Everyone was saying she had lost her looks badly of late, and was nothing like as pretty on her wedding day as she usually was; Levin did not see it that way. He looked at her hair piled up high under the long white veil and the white flowers, at the high stand-up scalloped collar that hid her long neck on either side in such a girlish way and only let it show in front, at her strikingly slender figure, and it struck him that she had never looked better — not because the flowers, the veil, the gown from Paris added anything to her beauty, but because, in spite of the elaborate splendor of her dress, the look on her sweet face, in her eyes, on her lips was still her own particular expression of utter, unguarded truthfulness.
"I was starting to think you meant to run for it," she said, and smiled at him.
"What happened to me is so stupid, I'm ashamed to say it out loud," he said, going red, and he had to turn to Sergey Ivanovitch, who had come up beside him.
"That's a fine story of yours about the shirt!" Sergey Ivanovitch said, shaking his head and smiling.
"Yes, yes!" Levin answered, with no idea what they were talking about.

"Now, Kostya, you have a decision to make," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, with a put-on look of dismay, "a serious question. You're in just the right mood now to grasp how grave it is. They're asking me whether they should use candles that have already been lit before or candles that have never been lit. It's a question of ten roubles," he added, his lips relaxing into a smile. "I've already decided, but I was afraid you might disagree."
Levin saw it was a joke, but he could not smile.
"Well, which is it to be — unlit candles or lit ones? That's the question."
"Yes, yes, unlit."

"Oh, I'm very glad. Decision made!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling. "How silly men are, though, in this state," he said to Tchirikov, once Levin, after a vacant look at him, had moved back to his bride.
"Kitty, remember — you must be the first to step on the carpet," Countess Nordston said, coming up. "You're a fine one!" she added to Levin.
"You're not frightened, are you?" asked Marya Dmitrievna, an old aunt.
"Are you cold? You're pale. Hold still a moment, stoop down," said Kitty's sister, Madame Lvova, and with her plump, handsome arms she smilingly straightened the flowers on her head.
Dolly came over, tried to say something, couldn't get the words out, started crying, and then laughed in a forced way.
Kitty looked at all of them with the same absent eyes as Levin.

Meanwhile the officiating clergy had robed themselves, and the priest and deacon came out to the lectern at the front of the church. The priest turned to Levin and said something. Levin did not catch what he said.
"Take the bride's hand and lead her forward," the best man told Levin.

It took Levin a long time to work out what he was supposed to do. They kept trying to set him straight and making him start over, because he kept taking Kitty by the wrong arm or with the wrong arm — until finally he understood that, without shifting his position, he was to take her right hand in his right hand. Once he had finally taken her hand the correct way, the priest walked a few steps ahead of them and stopped at the lectern. The crowd of friends and relations followed after, with a hum of talk and a rustle of skirts. Someone bent down and pulled out the bride's train. The church became so quiet that the drops of wax could be heard falling from the candles.

The little old priest, in his clerical cap, his long silvery-gray locks parted behind his ears, was fussing with something on the lectern, his small old hands sticking out from beneath the heavy silver vestment with the gold cross stitched on its back.
Stepan Arkadyevitch went up to him carefully, whispered something, signaled to Levin, and walked back again.

The priest lit two candles wreathed in flowers, and holding them at an angle so the wax dripped slowly, he turned to face the bridal pair. The priest was the same old man who had heard Levin's confession. He looked at the bride and bridegroom with tired, melancholy eyes, sighed, drew his right hand out from under his vestment to bless the bridegroom, and with a touch of anxious tenderness laid his crossed fingers on Kitty's bowed head. Then he handed them the candles, took up the censer, and moved slowly away from them.

"Can this really be happening?" Levin thought, and he glanced sideways at his bride. Looking down, he saw her face in profile, and from the barely visible quiver of her lips and lashes he knew she felt his eyes on her. She did not look round, but the high scalloped collar that reached her little pink ear was trembling faintly. He saw that she was holding back a sigh in her throat, and that the small hand inside the long glove was shaking as it held the candle.
All the fuss over the shirt, the running late, all the talk of friends and relations, their irritation, his ridiculous position — all of it suddenly fell away, and he was filled with joy and dread.
The handsome, stately head-deacon in his silver robe, his curly hair standing out at the sides of his head, stepped briskly forward, lifted his stole on two fingers, and stood opposite the priest.
"Blessed be the name of the Lord," the solemn syllables rang out slowly, one after another, setting the air quivering with waves of sound.

"Blessed is the name of our God, from the beginning, now, and ever shall be," the little old priest answered in a submissive, piping voice, still fingering something at the lectern. And the full chorus of the unseen choir rose up, filling the whole church from the windows to the vaulted roof with broad waves of melody. It swelled, held for a moment, and slowly faded away.

They prayed, as they always do, for peace from on high and for salvation, for the Holy Synod, and for the Tsar; and they prayed too for the servants of God Konstantin and Ekaterina, who were now plighting their troth.
"Grant them love made perfect, peace and help, O Lord, we beseech Thee," — the whole church seemed to breathe along with the head deacon's voice.

Levin heard the words, and they struck him. "How did they guess that help is exactly what one needs — just help?" he thought, remembering all his recent fears and doubts. "What do I know? What can I do in this terrible business," he thought, "without help? Yes — help is what I need now."

When the deacon had finished the prayer for the Imperial family, the priest turned to the bridal pair with a book in his hand: "Eternal God, that joinest together in love them that were separate," he read in a gentle, piping voice, "who hast ordained the union of holy wedlock that cannot be set asunder, Thou who didst bless Isaac and Rebecca and their descendants, according to Thy Holy Covenant; bless Thy servants, Konstantin and Ekaterina, leading them in the path of all good works. For gracious and merciful art Thou, our Lord, and glory be to Thee, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, now and ever shall be."
"Amen!" the unseen choir sent rolling once again through the air.
"'Joinest together in love them that were separate.' What a deep meaning those words have, and how they match what one feels at this moment," Levin thought. "Is she feeling the same as I am?"

And looking round, he met her eyes, and from the look in them he decided she understood it just as he did. But he was wrong; she had almost completely missed the meaning of the words of the service — in fact, she had not heard them. She could not listen and take them in, so strong was the single feeling filling her chest and growing stronger and stronger. That feeling was joy at the completion of the process that for the last month and a half had been going on inside her, and that during those six weeks had been both a joy and a torment to her. On the day when, in the drawing room of the house on Arbaty Street, she had walked up to him in her brown dress and given herself to him without a word — on that day, at that hour, a clean break with all her old life had happened inside her, and a quite different, new, completely strange life had begun, even while the old life outwardly carried on as before. Those six weeks had been a time for her of the deepest bliss and the deepest misery. Her whole life, all her desires and hopes, were focused on this one man, still not understood by her, to whom she was bound by a feeling of attraction and repulsion that took turns, and that was even less understood than the man himself, and all the while she went on living in the outward circumstances of her old life. Living that old life, she was horrified at herself, at her utter, insurmountable indifference to her whole past, to things, to habits, to the people she had loved and who loved her — to her mother, who was hurt by her coldness, to her kind, tender father, until then dearer to her than anyone in the world. One moment she was horrified at this indifference, the next she was glad of whatever had brought her to it. She could not frame a thought or a wish apart from life with this man; but this new life was not here yet, and she could not even picture it clearly. There was only anticipation — the dread and the joy of the new and the unknown. And now, here it was — anticipation and uncertainty and remorse at the abandoning of the old life — all of it ending, and the new beginning. This new life could not help frightening her, given her inexperience; but frightening or not, the change had already been made six weeks ago in her soul, and this was simply the final seal on something long since completed in her heart.

Turning back to the lectern, the priest with some difficulty took Kitty's little ring, asked Levin for his hand, and slid it onto the first joint of his finger. "The servant of God, Konstantin, plights his troth to the servant of God, Ekaterina." And sliding the larger ring onto Kitty's touchingly slight, pink little finger, the priest said the same thing.

Several times the bridal pair tried to work out what they were supposed to do, and each time got it wrong and had to be corrected by the priest in a whisper. At last, having properly performed the ceremony, having signed the rings with the cross, the priest handed Kitty the big ring and Levin the little one. Again they were puzzled, and passed the rings back and forth from hand to hand, still without doing what was expected.

Dolly, Tchirikov, and Stepan Arkadyevitch stepped forward to set them right. There was a pause of hesitation, whispering, and smiles; but the look of solemn emotion on the faces of the betrothed pair did not change — on the contrary, in their bewilderment about their hands they looked even more grave and moved than before, and the smile with which Stepan Arkadyevitch whispered to them that they were each supposed to put on their own ring died on his lips. He felt that any smile would jar on them.

"Thou who didst from the beginning create male and female," the priest read after the exchange of rings, "from Thee woman was given to man to be a helpmeet to him, and for the procreation of children. O Lord, our God, who hast poured down the blessings of Thy Truth according to Thy Holy Covenant upon Thy chosen servants, our fathers, from generation to generation, bless Thy servants Konstantin and Ekaterina, and make their troth fast in faith, and union of hearts, and truth, and love...."

Levin felt more and more strongly that all his ideas about marriage, all his dreams of how he was going to arrange his life, were sheer childishness — that this was something he had never understood before and now understood less than ever, even though it was being done to him. The lump in his throat rose higher and higher, and tears he could not hold back came into his eyes.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: All of Moscow was in the church — every friend and relation; and through the ceremony of plighting troth, in the brilliantly lit church, there was a steady flow of discreet, lowered conversation in the circle of brightly dressed women and girls and the men in white ties, frock coats, and uniforms. The talking was kept up mainly by the men, while the women were absorbed in following every detail of the ceremony, which always means so much to them.
In the small group closest to the bride were her two sisters: Dolly, and the other one, the self-possessed beauty Madame Lvova, who had only just arrived from abroad.
"Why is Marie wearing lilac — practically as bad as black — at a wedding?" said Madame Korsunskaya.
"With her coloring, it's her only salvation," Madame Trubetskaya replied. "I wonder why they had the wedding in the evening? It's a shopkeeper kind of thing...."

"It's much prettier. I was married in the evening too..." answered Madame Korsunskaya, and she sighed, remembering how charming she had looked that day, and how absurdly in love her husband had been, and how different everything was now.

"They say if a man's best man more than ten times, he'll never marry. I wanted to make it my tenth, but the spot was already taken," said Count Siniavin to the pretty Princess Tcharskaya, who had her sights on him.

Princess Tcharskaya only answered with a smile. She was looking at Kitty, thinking about how and when she would stand in Kitty's place beside Count Siniavin, and how she would then remind him of his joke today.
Shtcherbatsky told the old maid of honor, Madame Nikolaeva, that he meant to set the crown on Kitty's chignon for luck.

"She shouldn't have worn a chignon," Madame Nikolaeva answered — she had long since made up her mind that if the elderly widower she was angling for ever married her, the wedding would be of the simplest sort. "I don't care for that kind of grandeur."

Sergey Ivanovitch was talking to Darya Dmitrievna, half-joking with her that the custom of going away after the wedding was becoming common because newly married people always felt a little ashamed of themselves.
"Your brother can be proud of himself. She's a marvel of sweetness. I believe you're envious."
"Oh, I'm over that, Darya Dmitrievna," he answered, and a melancholy, serious look suddenly came over his face.
Stepan Arkadyevitch was telling his sister-in-law his joke about divorce.
"The wreath needs straightening," she answered, not hearing him.
"What a shame she's lost her looks so badly," Countess Nordston said to Madame Lvova. "Still, he's not worth her little finger, is he?"

"Oh, I like him so much — and not just because he's my future _beau-frère_," Madame Lvova answered. "And how well he's handling himself! It's so hard, too, to come off well in a position like that — not to look ridiculous. And he isn't ridiculous, and he isn't putting anything on; you can see he's moved."
"You expected this, I take it?"
"More or less. She always cared for him."
"Well, we'll see which of them steps on the rug first. I warned Kitty."
"It will make no difference," said Madame Lvova; "we're all obedient wives — it runs in the family."
"Oh, I stepped on the rug before Vassily on purpose. And you, Dolly?"

Dolly was standing next to them; she heard them, but did not answer. She was deeply moved. The tears stood in her eyes, and she could not have spoken without crying. She was rejoicing for Kitty and Levin; thinking back to her own wedding, she glanced at Stepan Arkadyevitch's radiant figure, forgot the present entirely, and remembered only her own innocent love. She thought not only of herself but of all her women friends and acquaintances. She thought of them on that one day of their triumph, when each had stood like Kitty under the wedding crown, with love and hope and dread in her heart, renouncing the past and stepping forward into the mysterious future. Among the brides who came back to her memory she thought too of her darling Anna, whose proposed divorce she had just been hearing about. And she had stood there just as innocently in orange blossoms and a bridal veil. And now? "It's terribly strange," she said to herself. It was not only the sisters, women friends, and female relations of the bride who were following every detail of the ceremony. Women who were complete strangers, mere spectators, were watching it with excitement, holding their breath, afraid of missing a single movement or expression of the bride and bridegroom, and angrily not answering — often not even hearing — the remarks of the unfeeling men, who kept making joking or off-topic observations.
"Why has she been crying? Is she being married against her will?"
"Against her will, to a fine fellow like that? A prince, isn't he?"
"Is that her sister in the white satin? Just listen to the deacon boom out, 'And fearing her husband.'"
"Are the choristers from Tchudovo?"
"No, from the Synod."
"I asked the footman. He says he's taking her straight off to his country place. Frightfully rich, they say. That's why she's marrying him."
"No, they're a well-matched pair."

"I say, Marya Vassilievna, you were claiming those fly-away crinolines weren't being worn anymore. Just look at her in the puce dress — an ambassador's wife, they say — see how her skirt bounces side to side!"
"What a pretty dear the bride is — like a lamb decked in flowers! Well, say what you like, we women feel for our sister."
Such were the comments in the crowd of gawking women who had managed to slip in at the church doors.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: When the ceremony of plighting troth was over, the beadle spread a piece of pink silk on the floor in front of the lectern in the middle of the church, the choir sang an elaborate, complicated psalm in which bass and tenor sang responses to one another, and the priest turned and pointed the bridal pair toward the pink silk rug. Although both had often heard plenty about the saying that whoever steps on the rug first will be the head of the household, neither Levin nor Kitty was capable of remembering it as they took the few steps toward it. They did not hear the loud remarks and arguments that followed — some insisting he had stepped on first, others that they had stepped on together.

After the usual questions — whether they wished to enter into matrimony, and whether they were pledged to anyone else — and their answers, which sounded strange to them even as they gave them, a new ceremony began. Kitty listened to the words of the prayer, trying to catch their meaning, but she could not. The feeling of triumph and radiant happiness flooded her soul more and more as the ceremony went on, and made it impossible for her to pay attention.

They prayed: "Endow them with continence and fruitfulness, and vouchsafe that their hearts may rejoice looking upon their sons and daughters." They referred to God's creation of a wife from Adam's rib — "and for this cause a man shall leave father and mother, and cleave unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh," and that "this is a great mystery"; they prayed that God would make them fruitful and bless them, like Isaac and Rebecca, Joseph, Moses and Zipporah, and that they might see their children's children. "All of that is splendid," Kitty thought, catching the words, "it's all exactly as it should be," and a smile of happiness, unconsciously reflected on the face of everyone who looked at her, shone on her radiant face.

"Put it on properly!" voices were heard urging when the priest had set the wedding crowns in place and Shtcherbatsky, his hand shaking in its three-button glove, was holding the crown high above her head.
"Put it on!" she whispered, smiling.
Levin looked round at her, and was struck by the joyful radiance on her face, and without meaning to he caught her mood. He too, like her, felt glad and happy.

They enjoyed hearing the epistle read, and the roll of the head deacon's voice on the final verse, which the outside public had been waiting for so impatiently. They enjoyed drinking from the shallow cup of warm watered-down red wine, and they were still more pleased when the priest, flinging back his stole and taking both their hands in his, led them around the lectern to the accompaniment of bass voices chanting "Glory to God."

Shtcherbatsky and Tchirikov, holding the crowns and stumbling over the bride's train, smiling too and looking as though something had delighted them, were one moment left behind and the next stepping on the bridal pair as the priest came to a halt. The spark of joy lit in Kitty seemed to have infected everyone in the church. It seemed to Levin that the priest and the deacon wanted to smile just as he did.

Taking the crowns off their heads, the priest read the final prayer and congratulated the young people. Levin looked at Kitty, and he had never seen her look like this before. She was charming with the new radiance of happiness in her face. Levin longed to say something to her, but he did not know whether it was all over. The priest got him out of his difficulty. He smiled his kindly smile and said gently, "Kiss your wife, and you kiss your husband," and took the candles out of their hands.

Levin kissed her smiling lips with timid care, gave her his arm, and with a new, strange sense of closeness walked her out of the church. He did not believe it, could not believe, that it was real. It was only when their wondering, timid eyes met that he believed in it, because he felt that they were one.
After supper, that same night, the young couple left for the country.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Vronsky and Anna had been traveling together in Europe for three months. They had visited Venice, Rome, and Naples, and had just arrived at a small Italian town where they meant to stay for a while. A handsome head waiter — thick pomaded hair parted from the nape upwards, an evening coat, a broad white cambric shirt front, and a bunch of trinkets hanging above his rounded stomach — was standing with his hands buried in his pockets, his eyes contemptuously half-lidded as he gave some frigid reply to a gentleman who had stopped him. Catching the sound of footsteps coming from the other side of the entry toward the staircase, the head waiter turned, and seeing the Russian count, who had taken their best rooms, he took his hands out of his pockets deferentially, bowed, and told him that a courier had been and that the business about the palazzo was settled. The steward was ready to sign the agreement.
"Ah! I'm glad to hear it," said Vronsky. "Is madame in or out?"
"Madame went out for a walk, but has now returned," the waiter replied.

Vronsky took off his soft, wide-brimmed hat and ran his handkerchief over his hot forehead and over his hair, which had grown halfway over his ears and was brushed back to cover the bald patch. With a casual glance at the gentleman still standing there staring at him, he was about to walk on.
"This gentleman is a Russian, and was asking after you," said the head waiter.

With a mix of annoyance at never being able to escape acquaintances anywhere, and a longing for something to break the monotony of his life, Vronsky looked again at the gentleman, who had backed away and was standing still once more, and at the same instant a light came into both of their eyes.
"Golenishtchev!"
"Vronsky!"

It really was Golenishtchev, a former classmate of Vronsky's in the Corps of Pages. In the corps Golenishtchev had belonged to the liberal party; he had left the corps without going into the army and had never taken a government post. Vronsky and he had gone in completely different directions after leaving the corps, and had only met once since.

At that meeting Vronsky had picked up that Golenishtchev had adopted a sort of lofty, intellectually liberal stance, and was therefore inclined to look down on Vronsky's interests and line of life. Vronsky had accordingly met him with the chilling, haughty manner he knew so well how to put on, the message of which was: "You may like or dislike how I live, that is a matter of perfect indifference to me; you will have to treat me with respect if you want my acquaintance." Golenishtchev had been contemptuously indifferent to the tone Vronsky took. One would have supposed this second meeting would push them further apart still. But here they were, beaming and exclaiming with delight at recognizing one another. Vronsky would never have expected to be so glad to see Golenishtchev, but probably he was not himself aware of how bored he had been. He forgot the disagreeable impression of their last meeting, and with a face of frank delight held out his hand to his old comrade. The same expression of delight replaced the look of unease on Golenishtchev's face.
"How glad I am to see you!" said Vronsky, showing his strong white teeth in a friendly smile.
"I heard the name Vronsky, but I didn't know which one. I'm very, very glad!"
"Let's go in. Come, tell me what you're up to."
"I've been living here for two years. I'm working."
"Ah!" said Vronsky, with sympathy. "Let's go in." And in the habit Russians have of not wanting the servants to overhear what they want to keep private in Russian, he switched into French.
"Do you know Madame Karenina? We're traveling together. I'm just going to see her," he said in French, watching Golenishtchev's face carefully.
"Ah! I didn't know" (though he did know), Golenishtchev answered casually. "Have you been here long?" he added.
"Four days," Vronsky answered, scrutinizing his friend's face again.

"Yes, he's a decent fellow, and will take the thing properly," Vronsky said to himself, catching the meaning of Golenishtchev's expression and his change of subject. "I can introduce him to Anna — he takes the right view."

Over the three months Vronsky had spent abroad with Anna, he had always, on meeting new people, asked himself how the new person would see his relations with Anna, and for the most part, in men, he had been met with the "proper" view of it. But if he had been asked — and if those who took it "properly" had been asked — to spell out exactly how they saw it, both he and they would have been at a loss to answer.

In reality, those who in Vronsky's mind took the "proper" view had no view at all, and were behaving in general the way well-bred people behave toward all the complicated, unsolvable problems life surrounds them with on all sides: behaving with propriety, avoiding allusions and awkward questions. They put on an air of fully grasping the meaning and weight of the situation, of accepting and even approving of it, but of regarding it as superfluous and uncalled-for to put any of this into words.

Vronsky guessed at once that Golenishtchev was of this kind, and was doubly pleased to see him on that account. And in fact Golenishtchev's manner toward Madame Karenina, when he was taken to call on her, was all Vronsky could have wished. He clearly steered clear of any subject that might lead to awkwardness, and without the slightest visible effort.

He had never met Anna before, and was struck by her beauty, and still more by the frankness with which she accepted her position. She blushed when Vronsky brought Golenishtchev in, and he was thoroughly charmed by this childlike blush spreading over her open, handsome face. What he liked particularly was the way she at once — as if on purpose to head off any misunderstanding with an outsider — called Vronsky simply Alexey, and said they were moving into a house they had just taken, what was called here a palazzo. Golenishtchev liked this direct, simple attitude toward her own position. Watching Anna's manner of frank, lively gaiety, and knowing both Alexey Alexandrovitch and Vronsky, Golenishtchev imagined he understood her perfectly. He imagined he understood what she herself was utterly unable to understand: how it was that, having made her husband miserable, having abandoned him and her son and lost her good name, she could still feel full of spirits, gaiety, and happiness.
"It's in the guidebook," said Golenishtchev, referring to the palazzo Vronsky had taken. "There's a first-rate Tintoretto in it. One from his late period."
"I'll tell you what — it's a lovely day, let's go and have another look at it," said Vronsky, turning to Anna.

"I'd love to; I'll just go and put on my hat. Would you say it's hot out?" she said, stopping short in the doorway and giving Vronsky a questioning look. And again a vivid flush spread across her face.
Vronsky saw from her eyes that she did not know on what terms he wished to be with Golenishtchev, and so was afraid of not behaving the way he would want.
He gave her a long, tender look.
"No, not very," he said.
And it seemed to her that she had grasped everything — above all that he was pleased with her; and smiling at him, she walked out the door with her quick step.

The two friends glanced at each other, and a hesitant look came into both their faces, as though Golenishtchev, plainly admiring her, would have liked to say something about her and could not find the right thing to say, while Vronsky both wanted him to say it and dreaded him doing so.

"Well then," Vronsky began, trying to start up some kind of conversation, "so you're settled here? You're still at the same work, then?" he went on, remembering he had heard Golenishtchev was writing something.

"Yes, I'm writing the second part of the _Two Elements_," said Golenishtchev, coloring with pleasure at the question — "that is, to be exact, I'm not writing it yet; I'm preparing, gathering material. It will be on a much wider scale, and will touch on nearly every question. We in Russia refuse to see that we are the heirs of Byzantium," — and he launched into a long, heated exposition of his views.

Vronsky was at first embarrassed at not even knowing about the first part of the _Two Elements_, which the author spoke of as something well known. But as Golenishtchev began laying out his opinions, and Vronsky found he could follow them even without knowing the _Two Elements_, he listened with some interest, because Golenishtchev spoke well. But Vronsky was startled and put off by the nervous irritability with which Golenishtchev talked about the subject that absorbed him. As he went on talking, his eyes glittered angrier and angrier; he was more and more hurried in his replies to imaginary opponents, and his face grew more and more agitated and worried. Remembering Golenishtchev as a thin, lively, good-natured, well-bred boy who was always at the top of the class, Vronsky could not make out why he was so irritated, and he did not like it. What he particularly disliked was that Golenishtchev, a man from a good set, would put himself on the same level with some hack writers, with whom he was irritated and angry. Was it worth it? Vronsky did not like it, but he felt that Golenishtchev was unhappy and was sorry for him. Unhappiness, almost mental disturbance, was visible in his mobile, rather handsome face, while without even noticing Anna's coming in he hurried on hotly setting out his views.

When Anna came in in her hat and cape, her lovely hand swinging her parasol with quick movements, and stood beside him, it was with a feeling of relief that Vronsky tore himself away from Golenishtchev's plaintive eyes, which kept fastening on him, and with a fresh rush of love looked at his charming companion, full of life and happiness. Golenishtchev pulled himself together with an effort, and at first was downcast and gloomy, but Anna, in the mood she was in then to be friendly with everyone, soon revived his spirits with her direct, lively manner. After trying out several subjects, she got him talking about painting, on which he spoke very well, and she listened to him attentively. They walked over to the house they had taken and looked it over.

"I'm so glad of one thing," said Anna to Golenishtchev when they were on the way back. "Alexey will have a wonderful _atelier_. You absolutely must take that room," she said to Vronsky in Russian, using the affectionately familiar form, as if she had seen that Golenishtchev would become close to them in their isolation and there was no point in being reserved in front of him.
"You paint?" said Golenishtchev, turning round quickly to Vronsky.
"Yes, I used to study it long ago, and now I've started doing a bit again," said Vronsky, going red.
"He has great talent," said Anna with a delighted smile. "I'm no judge, of course. But good judges have said the same thing."

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Anna, in that first period of her emancipation and her quick return to health, felt unforgivably happy and full of the joy of life. The thought of her husband's unhappiness did not poison her happiness. On one side that memory was too dreadful to be looked at. On the other side, her husband's unhappiness had given her too much happiness to be regretted. The memory of everything that had happened after her illness — her reconciliation with her husband, its breakdown, the news of Vronsky's wound, his visit, the preparations for divorce, the leaving of her husband's house, the parting from her son — all of it seemed to her like a feverish dream from which she had woken up alone with Vronsky abroad. The thought of the harm done to her husband stirred a feeling in her like revulsion, something like what a drowning man might feel after shaking off another man who was clinging to him. That man did drown. It was a wicked act, of course, but it was the only way out, and better not to brood over such terrible facts.

One consoling reflection on her behavior had come to her at the very moment of the final break, and now, recalling all the past, she remembered that one thought. "I have unavoidably made that man miserable," she thought, "but I don't want to profit by his misery. I too am suffering, and shall suffer; I'm losing what I valued above everything — I'm losing my good name and my son. I've done wrong, and so I don't want happiness, I don't want a divorce, and shall suffer from my disgrace and from being separated from my child." But however sincerely Anna had meant to suffer, she was not suffering. There was no shame. With the tact both of them had in such large supply, they had managed to avoid Russian ladies abroad, and so had never put themselves in a false position, and everywhere they had met people who pretended to understand their situation perfectly — far better, in fact, than they did themselves. Separation from the son she loved — even that did not cause her real anguish in these early days.
