The baby girl — _his_ child — was so sweet, and had so won Anna's heart, being all that was left to her, that Anna rarely thought of her son.

The desire for life, growing stronger with her recovered health, was so intense, and the circumstances of life were so new and pleasant, that Anna felt unforgivably happy. The more she got to know Vronsky, the more she loved him. She loved him both for himself and for his love of her. To have him completely her own was a continuous joy. His presence was always sweet to her. Every trait of his character, which she came to know better and better, was unspeakably dear to her. His appearance, changed by civilian dress, was as attractive to her as if she were a young girl in love. In everything he said, thought, and did, she saw something especially noble and elevated. Her adoration of him alarmed her, in fact; she searched in him for anything that wasn't fine, and could not find it. She did not dare let him see her sense of how insignificant she was beside him. She felt that, if he knew, he might stop loving her sooner; and she dreaded nothing now so much as losing his love, even though she had no reason to fear it. But she could not help being grateful to him for the way he treated her, and showing that she appreciated it. He, who in her view had such a clear gift for a political career — one in which he would certainly have played a leading part — had sacrificed his ambition for her sake, and never showed the slightest sign of regret. He was more lovingly respectful to her than ever, and his constant care that she should never feel the awkwardness of her position never left him for a single instant. He, so manly a man, never opposed her — indeed had no will of his own with her, and was anxious, it seemed, for nothing but to anticipate her wishes. And she could not help appreciating this, even though the very intensity of his concern for her, the atmosphere of care he surrounded her with, sometimes weighed on her.

Vronsky, meanwhile, in spite of the complete realization of what he had so long wanted, was not perfectly happy. He soon felt that the realization of his desires had given him no more than a grain of sand out of the mountain of happiness he had been expecting. It showed him the mistake men make in picturing happiness as the realization of their desires. For a time after joining his life to hers and putting on civilian dress, he had felt all the delight of freedom in general, which he had known nothing of before, and of freedom in his love — and he was content, but not for long. He soon realized that there was springing up in his heart a desire for desires — _ennui_. Without meaning to, he began grasping at every passing whim, mistaking it for a desire and an object. Sixteen hours of the day had to be filled somehow, since they were living abroad in complete freedom, outside the framework of social life that filled up the time in Petersburg. As for the amusements of bachelor existence, which had kept Vronsky entertained on previous trips abroad, those were out of the question, since the one attempt of the kind had led to a sudden bout of depression in Anna, quite out of proportion to its cause — a late supper with bachelor friends. Relations with the local society — foreign and Russian — were equally out of the question, given the irregularity of their position. Sightseeing — apart from the fact that everything had already been seen — did not, for Vronsky, a Russian and a sensible man, carry the enormous significance Englishmen are able to attach to it.
And just as a hungry stomach eagerly seizes on anything it can get, hoping to find nourishment in it, Vronsky, quite unconsciously, grabbed first at politics, then at new books, then at pictures.

Since he had had a taste for painting from childhood, and since, not knowing what else to spend his money on, he had started collecting engravings, he came to a stop at painting, began to take an interest in it, and concentrated on it the unoccupied mass of desires that were demanding satisfaction.

He had a quick eye for art, and probably, with his taste for imitating art, he supposed himself to have the real thing that's essential for an artist — and after some hesitation over which style of painting to pick — religious, historical, realistic, or genre painting — he set to work to paint. He could appreciate all kinds and could have felt inspired by any of them; but he had no conception of the possibility of knowing nothing at all about any school of painting, and of being inspired directly by what is inside one's soul, without minding whether what one paints belongs to any recognized school. Since he knew nothing of this, and drew his inspiration not directly from life but indirectly from life as embodied in art, his inspiration came very quickly and easily, and just as quickly and easily came his success in painting something very similar to the kind of painting he was trying to imitate.

More than any other style, he liked the French — graceful and effective — and in that style he began painting Anna's portrait in Italian costume, and the portrait seemed to him, and to everyone who saw it, extremely successful.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: The old neglected palazzo, with its lofty carved ceilings and frescoed walls, its mosaic floors, its heavy yellow stuff curtains on the windows, its vases on pedestals and open fireplaces, its carved doors and gloomy reception rooms hung with paintings — this palazzo did a great deal, by its very appearance after they had moved in, to confirm in Vronsky the pleasing illusion that he was not so much a Russian country gentleman and retired army officer as an enlightened amateur and patron of the arts — himself a modest artist who had given up the world, his connections, and his ambition for the woman he loved.

The pose Vronsky chose after they moved into the palazzo was a complete success, and, having made the acquaintance through Golenishtchev of a few interesting people, he was content for a time. He painted studies from nature under the guidance of an Italian professor of painting, and studied medieval Italian life. Medieval Italian life so fascinated Vronsky that he even took to wearing a hat and flinging a cloak over his shoulder in the medieval style, which actually suited him very well.

"Here we are living, and we know nothing of what's going on," Vronsky said to Golenishtchev when he came in one morning to see him. "Have you seen Mihailov's picture?" he said, handing him a Russian newspaper he had received that morning and pointing to an article about a Russian artist who was living in the same town and just finishing a picture that had been talked about for a long time and had already been bought in advance. The article reproached the government and the academy for leaving such a remarkable artist without encouragement or support.

"I've seen it," Golenishtchev answered. "Of course, he's not without talent, but it's all heading in the wrong direction. It's the whole Ivanov-Strauss-Renan attitude toward Christ and toward religious painting."
"What's the subject of the picture?" asked Anna.
"Christ before Pilate. Christ is shown as a Jew, with all the realism of the new school."
And the question of the subject having brought him onto one of his favorite theories, Golenishtchev launched into a full speech on it.

"I can't understand how they fall into such a gross error. Christ always has his definite embodiment in the art of the great masters. So if they want to depict not God but a revolutionary or a sage, let them take a Socrates or a Franklin or a Charlotte Corday from history — but not Christ. They take the one figure that can't be used for their kind of art, and then...."
"And is it true that this Mihailov is in such poverty?" asked Vronsky, thinking that, as a Russian Mæcenas, it was his duty to help the artist, whether the picture turned out to be good or bad.

"I don't think so. He's a remarkable portrait painter. Have you ever seen his portrait of Madame Vassiltchikova? But I gather he doesn't care to paint any more portraits, and so very likely he is short of money. I maintain that...."
"Couldn't we ask him to paint a portrait of Anna Arkadyevna?" said Vronsky.

"Why mine?" said Anna. "After yours, I don't want another portrait. Better have one of Annie" (that was what she called her baby girl). "Here she is," she added, looking out of the window at the handsome Italian nurse, who was carrying the child out into the garden, and immediately glancing — without anyone noticing — at Vronsky. The handsome nurse, from whom Vronsky was painting a head for his picture, was the one hidden sorrow in Anna's life. He worked with her as his model, admired her beauty and her medieval look, and Anna did not dare admit to herself that she was afraid of becoming jealous of this nurse, and was for that reason particularly gracious and considerate to both her and her little son. Vronsky too looked out the window and into Anna's eyes, and, turning at once to Golenishtchev, said:
"Do you know this Mihailov?"

"I've met him. But he's an odd fish, and quite without breeding. You know, one of those uncouth new people one runs across so often nowadays, one of those free-thinkers, the kind who are reared _d'emblée_ on theories of atheism, scepticism, and materialism. In the old days," Golenishtchev went on, not noticing — or not wanting to notice — that both Anna and Vronsky were trying to speak, "in the old days the free-thinker was a man who had been brought up on ideas of religion, law, and morality, and only through conflict and struggle came to free thought; but now a new type has sprung up — born free-thinkers, who grow up without ever having heard of principles of morality or religion, of the existence of authorities, who grow up directly in the ideas of negation about everything — that is to say, savages. Well, he belongs to that class. He's the son, apparently, of some Moscow butler, and never had any sort of upbringing. When he got into the academy and made his reputation, he tried, as he's no fool, to educate himself. And he turned to what looked to him like the very source of culture — the magazines. In the old days, you see, a man who wanted to educate himself — a Frenchman, for instance — would have set about studying all the classics and theologians and tragedians and historians and philosophers — you know, all the intellectual work he could lay hands on. But in our day he goes straight for the literature of negation, very quickly absorbs all the digests of the science of negation, and he's done. And that's not all — twenty years ago he would still have found traces in that literature of struggle with authorities, with the creeds of the ages; he would have seen from that struggle that there was something else; but now he runs straight into a literature in which the old creeds don't even come up for discussion — it's simply stated flatly that there is nothing else — evolution, natural selection, struggle for existence — and that's the whole story. In my article I've...."

"I'll tell you what," said Anna, who had for some time been exchanging wary glances with Vronsky and knew that he was not in the least interested in the education of this artist but was simply taken up with the idea of helping him and ordering a portrait from him; "I'll tell you what," she said, resolutely cutting in on Golenishtchev, who was still talking away, "let's go and see him!"
Golenishtchev recovered his composure and readily agreed. But since the artist lived in a distant suburb, it was decided that they should take the carriage.

An hour later, Anna, with Golenishtchev beside her and Vronsky on the front seat of the carriage facing them, drove up to a new, ugly house in the remote suburb. Learning from the porter's wife, who came out to them, that Mihailov did receive visitors at his studio, but that at the moment he was at his lodging only a couple of steps away, they sent her over to him with their cards, asking permission to see his picture.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: The artist Mihailov was, as always, at work when the cards of Count Vronsky and Golenishtchev were brought in. In the morning he had been working in his studio on his big picture. On getting home, he had flown into a rage with his wife for not having managed to fend off the landlady, who had been asking for money.

"I've told you twenty times — don't get into details with her. You're foolish enough at the best of times, and when you start explaining things in Italian you're three times the fool," he said after a long argument.
"Then don't let it run on so long; it's not my fault. If I had the money...."

"Leave me alone, for God's sake!" Mihailov shrieked, tears in his voice, and clapping his hands over his ears he stalked off into his workroom on the other side of a partition wall and shut the door behind him. "Idiotic woman!" he muttered to himself, sat down at the table, opened a portfolio, and at once set to work with peculiar intensity on a sketch he had started.

He never worked with such fervor and success as when things were going badly for him, and especially when he had quarreled with his wife. "Oh — the devil take them all!" he thought as he went on working. He was making a sketch for the figure of a man in a violent rage. There was an earlier version of it, but he had been dissatisfied with it. "No, that other one was better ... where is it?" He went back to his wife, and scowling, not looking at her, asked his eldest little girl where that piece of paper was that he had given them. The paper with the discarded sketch on it was found, but it was dirty, with candle-grease spots on it. Still, he took the sketch, laid it on his table, and, stepping back a little and screwing up his eyes, he fell to gazing at it. All at once he smiled and gestured gleefully.
"That's it! That's it!" he said, and at once picking up his pencil he began drawing rapidly. The spot of tallow had given the man a new pose.

He had sketched this new pose when all at once he remembered the face of a shopkeeper from whom he had bought cigars, a vigorous face with a prominent chin, and he sketched that very face, that very chin, onto the figure of the man. He laughed aloud with delight. From a lifeless thing of his imagination the figure had become alive, and become something that could never be changed. That figure was living, and was clearly and unmistakably defined. The sketch could be corrected to suit the demands of the figure — the legs, in fact, could and must be set differently, and the position of the left hand had to be entirely changed; the hair too could be thrown back. But in making those corrections he was not changing the figure but only stripping away what was hiding it. He was, in effect, peeling off the wrappings that kept it from being clearly seen. Each new touch only brought out the whole figure in all its force and vigor, as it had suddenly come to him from the spot of tallow. He was carefully finishing the figure when the cards were brought in to him.
"Coming, coming!"
He went in to his wife.

"Come, Sasha, don't be cross!" he said, smiling at her timidly and affectionately. "You were to blame. I was to blame. I'll make it all right." And having made peace with his wife, he put on an olive-green overcoat with a velvet collar and a hat, and headed for his studio. The successful figure he had already forgotten. Now he was delighted and excited at the visit of these people of consequence, Russians, who had come in their carriage.

About his picture — the one now standing on his easel — he had at the bottom of his heart one conviction: that no one had ever painted a picture like it. He did not believe his picture was better than all of Raphael's, but he knew that what he was trying to convey in that picture no one had ever conveyed. This he knew for certain, and had known for a long time — ever since he had begun painting it. But other people's criticisms, whatever they might be, still had enormous weight in his eyes, and they shook him to the depths of his soul. Any remark, even the most insignificant, that showed the critic had seen even the tiniest part of what he saw in the picture shook him to the depths of his soul. He always attributed to his critics a deeper understanding than he had himself, and always expected from them something he could not see in the picture himself. And often in their criticisms he imagined he had found just that.

He walked rapidly to the door of his studio, and despite his excitement was struck by the soft light on Anna's figure as she stood in the shade of the entrance listening to Golenishtchev, who was eagerly telling her something, while she clearly wanted to glance over at the artist. He was unconscious himself of how, as he approached them, he seized on this impression and absorbed it, just as he had the chin of the shopkeeper who had sold him the cigars, and stored it away somewhere to be brought out when he needed it. The visitors, not favorably predisposed beforehand by Golenishtchev's account of the artist, were even less so by his appearance. Thick-set and of middle height, with quick movements, in his brown hat, olive-green coat, and narrow trousers — even though wide trousers had long been in fashion — and, above all, with the ordinariness of his broad face and the mixed expression of timidity and anxious self-importance, Mihailov made an unpleasant impression.
"Please step in," he said, trying to look indifferent, and going into the passage he took a key out of his pocket and unlocked the door.
